subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is the sad task of Parliament today to pay tribute to the memory of one of its most distinguished former members. The passing of David Lewis has deprived Canada of a man of passionate commitment, a man of ideas and conscience, a brilliant and eloquent person, a man who devoted the whole of his adult life to the service of others.
Canada's loss is felt nowhere more keenly than here in Parliament, a place he loved and honoured. It was here, as Leader of the New Democratic Party, that he found the fullest scope for the expression of his ideals and idealism. It was here that he was able to speak to Canadians, day in and day out, about social and economic justice, about the gap between what Canada was and could become, about the primary duty of Parliament to help and protect those who could not protect themselves.
By giving expression to his own profound belief that political action is the noblest and most effective means of achieving social change, he also lent added dignity and respect to the profession of politics, and to the Canadian political process.
Because he became best known to Canadians during his tenure as Leader of the New Democratic Party, it is sometimes forgotten that he was a political activist in the cause of social democracy for some forty-four years of his life.
His was a life-long commitment, played out principally away from the limelight of the national leadership, in the hard-slogging and frugal years organizing, travelling, and speaking in every part of Canada.
It was that commitment which gave power and forcefulness to his public performance. He was not one to play at politics for a time while waiting for more lucrative doors to open. He gave his life to politics, as his chosen way of giving his life to his country and its people.
David Lewis was a man in whom social idealism was combined with the most practical of political skills. He excelled as a strategist and orator, as a campaigner and organizer.
He knew every detail of the cost of every victory he won, because he had paid that cost in his own hard work.
He was a proud Canadian, imbued with the sense of wonder of one who was not born in this country. He both shamed and inspired many native-born Canadians by learning not just one of our official languages, but both of them, and he spoke them fluently. That was also a sign of his commitment to Canada and to all its people.
As we mourn the passing of this dedicated human being, our sympathy goes out to his beloved wife, Sophie, and to his family. May the knowledge of the great respect he earned throughout a life of service to Canada comfort them in this time of bereavement.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to associate my leader and my party with the tributes being paid to David Lewis today.
David Lewis was a person who cared. It was evident in everything he did throughout his life. He cared about people and wanted to see their hopes and aspirations met. He cared about principles and strove to uphold them in his personal and public life. He cared about Canada and returned, in full measure, the opportunities and advantages this country afforded him.
David Lewis was an ardent socialist, and this led him to a life-long association with the working people of Canada. In union halls, in mining communities, in fishing hamlets and, finally, in Parliament, he argued their cause, passionately and persuasively. He could do it because he knew them so well. He met them in their homes and wherever working people gather in this country.
David Lewis was guided by his principles. He rejected inequality and injustice wherever they occurred, and strove to banish them. In his own words, he saw democracy as a dynamic weapon in the war against poverty, prejudice, and ignorance. He had a deep and abiding belief in civil liberties, and was willing to stand up and be counted no matter what the personal and political cost.
David Lewis saw in Canada a country where the principles he espoused so strongly and the convictions he held so firmly would be embodied in the law and life of the land. He never doubted that that would come to pass in Canada.
As with many new members who entered the House in which he was already a veteran, I was deeply impressed by the power of his oratory, his skill in debate, and the force and conviction with which he participated in the work of this chamber. It was indeed an inspiration to a new member to

May 25, 1981
The Late David Lewis
listen to both our official languages being used in a manner both persuasive and effective, and indeed it was a challenge to all of us to try to improve our performance.
David Lewis was a great parliamentarian and a great Canadian. His work in this House and elsewhere is his lasting legacy to Canada. We join with all members in expressing our sorrow at his passing, and our sympathy to his family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER LEADER OF THE NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are most grateful to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). Indeed, we are most grateful to the House for taking these few moments to remember the life and work of our friend whom we have lost, David Lewis.
I express that gratitude on behalf of our leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), who will be interrupting his mission in Central America to be here tomorrow for the funeral service. I express it on behalf of all the members of our caucus and all our members and supporters across the country. In particular, however, I want to express appreciation on behalf of the members of David Lewis's family. I am grateful to both of those who preceded me for mentioning them.
We are all aware of David Lewis's public life. We are particularly aware of the crowning achievement of that life in the years that he spent as a leader in this House. What is perhaps not so generally known is that he was a warm and devoted family man. He was extremely happy to be with his wife Sophie, his four children, Stephen, Michael, Janet and Nina, with their spouses, with his six grandchildren, his sister Doris and her two children. I am sure it will mean much to all of them that the sympathy of this House has been expressed today by the Deputy Prime Minister and by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands who indeed were speaking on behalf of all of us.
We welcome the tributes that have been paid to the way in which David Lewis lived his life. We all know what a brilliant person he was, that he could have been a success in anything to which he turned his hand, but he believed so deeply in the right of common people to have a better life that he literally gave his life in their service in the political movement which he thought was best fitted to do just that.
As a party, we owe a debt to him for the organizational skills that he used to make our movement an effective force in the country. I believe the country is better off for there being the kind of democracy we have today, much of which is due to the impression made by our former leader. It is particularly fitting that this man who, as the Deputy Prime Minister said, spent many decades behind the scenes, was here as our party's leader during a couple of years when much of what he believed in was accomplished.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, we think today of the loss the family has sustained, we think of the loss that our movement
and our country have sustained, but we are also conscious of the fact that David Lewis was one who lived life in the very best way. Indeed, we are happy today, though we mourn his passing, to celebrate a life well lived.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF FOREIGN MANUFACTURED SCALES AND MEASURES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek unanimous approval on a very important matter. The metrication program of the government requires thousands of retail outlets in Canada to convert to metric over the next number of months. This will require hundreds of millions of dollars worth of scales and other measuring devices to be purchased by these retailers. Since these purchases must be made over the next number of months, this will prohibit the sourcing of these from Canadian manufacturers and suppliers. Therefore, due to the government's metric policy we are creating jobs in foreign countries and manufacturing opportunities for foreign companies. Last week in committee the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) indicated that this is the price we have to pay for metrication.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky):
That this House unanimously support the nomination of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce for the 1981 sell-out Canada award.

Madam Speaker, I know the minister would like us to believe that there are no bankruptcies in Canada, but if he would get out across Canada and talk to people, as I advised him more than a week ago, he would really find out what is happening. In the meantime, I refer him to a statement of one of his aides which came out of his office while he was away, about what would be done for home owners in the face of staggering mortgage rates. It was said:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for ignoring the consequences of its high interest rate policy and for its failure to assist the small business sector in Canada
(1)	by increasing and extending the small business development bond program;
(2)	by encouraging venture capital investment by means of appropriate tax adjustments;
(3)	by relieving the small business sector from the massive weight of government regulation; and
(4)	by fostering the research and development necessary to preserve the vitality of Canadian businesses of all sizes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, our motion sets forth the four main requirements if the small business sector is to survive and play its traditional role in our economy. That role is reflected by the fact that the small business sector is the largest employer in Canada, that it contributes a large percentage of the GNP to the national economy and the small business sector gives stability to the labour market because it traditionally retains its labour force when the market turns down.
The motion bears reading again:
That this House condemns the government for ignoring the consequences of its high interest policy and for its failure to assist the small business sector in Canada
Small Business
(1)	by increasing and extending the small business development bond program;
(2)	by encouraging venture capital investment by means of appropriate tax adjustments;
(3)	by relieving the small business sector from the massive weight of government regulation; and
(4)	by fostering the research and development necessary to preserve the vitality of Canadian business of all sizes.
The small business development bond is a good program but it must be extended. It should include unincorporated small businesses, farmers and fishermen. Where does the small businessman initially get his capital to start his business? He borrows it, or at least borrows to supplement his savings, or he cashes his life insurance, bonds or other assets, or he mortgages his house; and in many cases he does all of those things to accumulate enough capital to get going. He does this because he believes he has an idea that will be profitable or a service to render from which he feels he can make a reasonable fee.
If he is successful, how does he expand? In most cases an expansion of the small business is paid for out of retained earnings that are poured back into the business. Unless the small businessman becomes large enough to go public, he must find the capital for expansion from profits earned by the business or by borrowing from the bank.
The banks have not been all that helpful, particularly since capital gains have been imposed. Why do hon. members think the government introduced the Small Businesses Loans Act in 1960? It did so because the chartered banks were reluctant to make loans to small businesses. Even after the government guaranteed the loans, you could hardly find a bank that would admit such an act was in place. I could not begin to count the number of times small businessmen came to me complaining that their bank manager had never heard of the Small Businesses Loans Act or said he would have to check with his head office. However, once the rate for the loan moved to the current bank rate, the managers suddenly found the Small Businesses Loans Act in their files. While the rate was fixed lower by the government the banks were not interested; once it moved up to the current rate they became very interested.
The small businessman cannot survive the 19.6 per cent prime rate. The supply side of our economy is good, competition is strong, but inflation and increases in the rate of interest small businessmen must pay for the use of bank money is draining away these profits. What will happen is that inventories will drop and that drop will be rolled back onto the manufacturing side of our economy where the slowdown will be felt at a later time. The small business development bond must be extended to encompass the unincorporated businesses of farmers and fishermen and the term for repayment should be extended to ten years to allow for the regeneration of the small business sector.
If some relief, as suggested in my remarks, is not put in place and quickly, there will be a dramatic increase in bankruptcies. A bankruptcy is an economic tragedy. It is the cessation of the economic activity of an enterprise that means loss of employment, the loss of a contribution to the GNP, the

May 25, 1981
Small Business
loss of profits and, consequently, a loss to the tax base for three levels of government. If you are startled by the latest bankruptcy figures, Mr. Speaker, you will be really upset at the bankruptcies to come if some relief is not felt in the weeks ahead.
We have more than one million unemployed. The government talks about the work it has done in job creation. The reality is that many of those jobs are temporary. They are meant to get people into the labour force in the hope that they will stick. Most stick long enough to qualify for unemployment insurance, so they become a traveller between the employed and the unemployed.
One of the realities of the labour market is that the direction is the reverse to what most people believe. Many people are worried by automation in assembly operations. They fear automation and believe they may be replaced by a robot or some automatic assembly operation. The reality is that the fully employed worker of the future will be multitalented. He or she will be required to do several jobs and could move to a variety of employment. Some work will be performed in the home on computer terminals. That is almost a fact today.
If I had my way I would search out the most talented craftsmen in the world and bring them to Canada to teach their crafts to Canadians. The demand for the multitalented employee is growing. They are the core of the labour force in the small business sector. That is where the real strength is. They remain employed because they can turn their hands and head to a variety of jobs. They become indispensable to the small businessman. There is great vigour in the small business sector. That vigour and initiative must be matched with venture capital if it is to contribute to the economy in the very positive way it can.
Venture capital will only be made available with tax adjustments. The prospect of an unusual gain is the main reason people are willing to put venture capital on the line. The gain should be in the form of a non-taxable profit. There are as many ideas for venture capital formation as there are needs for it. Appropriate tax adjustments must be made to increase the flow of venture capital to the small business sector.
The plan I prefer is one developed by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. That plan, in short, allows the person lending the money to write off the loan from his tax payable and would cause him to pay income tax on the return when it is repaid. There are a number of variations of that idea, but it is one simple way of channelling venture capital funds to the small business sector. If you want a future for small business, Mr. Speaker, you have to buy it today. We can develop from the tinkerer-inventor-scientist dream if we are prepared to put venture capital on the line.
Let me say a few words about profit, because if anything has been maligned in the business world today it is profit. It should be looked upon as a tool with which to create the future. One of the great hang-ups of the socialists is that they love money but they hate profit. They would have you believe
that profits are stored in the corporate vaults and the boards of directors are groups of robbers who divvy up the profit at the expense of the worker. Anyone with an ounce of insight knows that profit is what is left over after all costs, including labour and taxes, are paid.
You have to look at profit in a different dimension. If you look at profit in the form of time, brain power and money you will see it is a tool to create the future. If we want social programs to continue to look after the unemployable and the elderly, they can only be sustained if we have profits. If we want to continue to improve our way of life and our standards of employment and living in the future, then we must do it by rethinking attitudes toward profits. As I said, most socialists love money but they hate profit. I make reference to socialists because the general public today believes the Liberal party is a socialist party. In fact, someone said to me the other day they are like the NDP in a hurry. That is a twist I am sure the House will recognize, and I knew that would get Stanley!
I wonder how many people really understand the effect of the massive weight of government regulation. I wonder how many realize the massive power in those regulations. If hon. members analyse the preamble to the average statute they debate in this House, they will find these words: "The governor in council shall attach regulations thereto upon proclamation". Further, they will see these words: "The governor in council may change regulations from time to time as required". From those two sentences the authority for regulations springs. You never see them until they are proclaimed in The Canada Gazette. They, are not exposed to anyone but the persons within the bureaucracy who use them.
Regulations have a life and power of their own. They are administered by faceless, nameless people who, for the most part, are removed from the mainstream of the realities of the businesses they would regulate. Let me give a few examples. The Metric Commission, in its haste to turn Canada into a metric nation, decided all gasoline service station air pumps should be converted to record air pressure in kilopascals rather than in pounds per square inch. A conversion program followed. I suppose in their fiddleheaded way they thought everyone was going to jump up and down with joy because they had made this great decision.
Let us look at the reality. A sign is placed on the air pump which tells you that the pump has been converted. The sign is in both official languages so you can have bilingual frustration. But no conversion chart tells you what 28 pounds per square inch converts to in kilopascals. I asked the service station operator when I happened to go in one day wanting to put some air in tires: "What do I put on the pump"? He was busy serving a customer and he said: "I don't know and I don't care. It's free air-why should I bother".
I called the Metric Commission and told them my dilemma. I said: "I am at a service station, the air pump is in kilopascals, my tires take 28 pounds per square inch; what does that convert to?" That created quite a problem. I waited on the phone for 45 minutes and Finally a voice said to me: "If you multiply 28 psi by 6.805 you will get the kilopascal setting to
May 25, 1981

put on the pump". I told him where to stuff the air pump, hose and all, it was such a frustrating experience.
A few years ago we had a bill before the House which dealt with tire standards. It had been drafted with the assistance of the rubber industry association and its member companies. Most people were satisfied with the safety standards set forth in the bill. In fact, the government was satisfied. Then the bureaucracy got hold of it and wanted to create a whole new layer of regulations. They were going to have every retail outlet in Canada and every gasoline station keep records of the serial numbers and the name and address of every person who purchased a tire. The retail store would then have to initiate a recall should one be required. In spite of the fact that the tire manufacturers said they would take over the responsibility, the bureaucracy pressed on.
In addition, they would have had a series of inspectors, they said, who would regularly check the retail tire sales outlets to see that the records were being properly kept. Can you imagine the bureaucracy you would have had in a city like Ottawa; probably half a dozen retail tire records inspectors who would probably have to report to a district inspector, who would report to an area inspector, who would report to a provincial inspector, who would report to an eastern-western inspector! It just goes on and on and on, and all to be paid for, of course, by the taxpayers. This would have laid upon the small retailers an unbelievable responsibility and, of course, additional overhead. We fought hard and we won that one. We had the provision withdrawn from the bill and left it with the industry to advise purchasers of recalls through their computer control system.
That measure came into the House of Commons by reason of the bureaucracy copying almost verbatim a statute that was in place in the United States. We had the same thing happen with some provisions under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act.
I recall when I first came to Ottawa in 1972 meeting with a trade association and Dr. Campbell who was head of the motor vehicle safety division in the Department of Transport. Dr. Campbell wanted to have some control over motor vehicles. In fact, the Motor Vehicle Safety Act used by the Government of Canada is word for word, page for page, clause for clause, item for item identical to the one used in the United States. All one has to do is take out the word "state" and insert the word "province" or "territory" and the acts are identical. In fact, one can work from the American legislation in Canada quite easily.
What we found happening was that Dr. Campbell wanted to make the last person who worked on a motor truck responsible for that total motor vehicle, regardless if he only hung a mud flap back of the tires, if he moved the turn signal back on the frame, or if he put anything on the vehicle, such as a reflector or another mirror. If he was the last person who worked on that $60,000 or $75,000 Mack truck, he was going to be responsible for the total recall of that vehicle if in fact a recall was required. In other words, Mack truck would advise a wee little operator that a certain vehicle was believed to have a defect. The small operator would have to go to the expense,
Small Business
time and trouble of notifying the purchaser of the vehicle that he must return it for a warranty repair.
It was a silly situation. We argued all day, and we finally convinced Dr. Campbell to back off; but his inspectors still go to little businesses around the country which do installation work on motor trucks. Those businesses are quite prepared to be responsible for what they instal, but they think it is ludicrous that they should be responsible for the total vehicle which was designed by General Motors, Ford, Mack truck or whoever it might be. That is the type of bureaucracy which drives people right up the wall.
The bureaucracy of government depends upon a passive Parliament to allow it full rein. If there is one non-partisan theme we all could look at, it is the effect of regulations on the public. This whole Parliament should be together on that. There should be no political partisanship whatever involved.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
We should be totally together. A rein should be put on this. Every country in the western world is faced with the same problem. We can see what is happening in the United States, which is attempting to deregulate. We have heard about regulation in Germany and in Japan. The bureaucracy gradually grows and grows until it swallows everyone. This Parliament would work better if we could spend a certain number of hours a week looking at regulations which are being introduced, even before they are put into The Canada Gazette. There should be references to an all-party committee. Such a committee could look at the regulations, rule on them or give its views on them before they are passed. There should be some type of review.
To go back to my story about tire inspectors, can hon. members imagine how many tire inspectors we would have in Canada if we had not stopped that measure? How many tires are damaged because of those idiots in the Metric Commission who decided that we should use kilopascals instead of pounds per square inch? Any safety expert or any tire shop operator can tell us that one of the greatest problems with tires is underinflation. Service station operators can tell us that the greatest trouble with bicycle tires is overinflation. If we go into any gasoline station, the operator can show us a line-up of blown bicycle tires.
The fact is that little, if anything, has been done to reduce regulations and paper loads respecting small businesses. I believe one of the previous ministers of state for small businesses set up a committee to look into the abuse of the small business community by means of paper work. I have not seen any results from that, but if the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) got together with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey), an income tax form could be devised on which all the information required by the government from the small business community could be gathered at the time income tax returns are filed. I am sure that could be done. It could be a once-a-year task. It could be

May 25, 1981
Small Business
kept simple and the amount of paper work kept to a minimum. That would stop Statistics Canada from calling and threatening small businessmen with fines if they do not send in certain returns by certain dates.
Let me turn to the fourth point in our motion respecting the fostering of research and development necessary to preserve the vitality of Canadian businesses of all sizes. Our contribution to research and development is one of the lowest of all OECD countries. It is far out of proportion to our labour force and the size of our primary and secondary industries. When we invest in research and development, we invest in the future. It seems to me that there is a mindset in the bureaucracy which firmly believes that the only new ideas we should use should come from outside Canada.
A former minister of state for science and technology-I believe he was also president of the treasury board at the same time-believed we could purchase our technology cheaper than we could develop it ourselves. I believe there are some in the Treasury Board and in the Department of Finance who still influence any move toward an expanded research and development program for industry. That kind of thinking will doom us forever to being a second or third-rate industrial nation. Some industries are large enough to have ongoing research and development programs of their own, but many undertake research and development only when their backs are to the wall.
I believe in the tinkerer-inventor-scientist theory that we have to begin somewhere. I have thought long and hard about the practical side of research and development funding. As I have stated many times in this House, the reality is that for all but a handful of industries which are large enough to sponsor full research and development programs the real problem is the availability of cash. The demands on profits and cash flow are so severe that research and development programs are shut down or never leave the ground in the first place.
I have suggested before in this House that we should put into place a registered research and development program. Under such a program a business could accumulate money for a period of time to ensure that funds are in place to undertake and complete a research and development program. The funds could be accumulated from a percentage of the tax payable and be drawn down once a project was decided upon by a business. We would find that an enormous amount of activity would ensue as a result of a program such as this. The government would not have to lay out $400 million or $500 million. The money would be drawn from the profits generated by a business, the government would hold the funds in a registered research and development trust fund and they could be drawn back by the business. That would allow businesses to complete projects which they want to get going.
There should be an emphasis on the training of technicians at community colleges. There should be more integrated programs with industry and, through a double write-off provision, businesses should be encouraged, wherever possible, to establish technical libraries. In the final analysis, we would be
investing in the future. We should do this with the sure knowledge that dividends would be returned many times over.
The motion before us is well thought out. I have attempted to give the House my thoughts in a positive, non-partisan manner. I believe the situation in the country today is very serious. This is a very serious motion, and it should be acted upon by the government with all possible speed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak in this Conservative opposition debate. This motion is indeed a thoughtful statement. It provides an opportunity for us to discuss some of the problems and challenges being faced by small businesses across Canada. Unfortunately, we seldom have an opportunity to discuss small business, and I am pleased to see the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) here today to listen to what opposition members have to say regarding that area of his portfolio. We look forward to hearing some new initiatives announced by the minister later this afternoon. We are anxious to hear what he has to say about the future of the small business community in Canada.
During these times there is no question that those who have been hardest hit by excessively high interest rates-the highest interest rates in Canadian history-have been people in the small business sector of our economy. For the more than
320.000 unincorporated small businesses and the more than
330.000	small and medium business corporations, interest rates of 19 and 20 per cent, now 21, 22 and 23 per cent, mean higher production costs and cutbacks in orders and inventory, which in turn mean lay-offs and production cuts for manufacturers and suppliers. Entrepreneurs and individuals interested in expansion and in seeing their businesses grow simply find that impossible with interest rates in the 20 plus percentile range. At a time when investment is crucial to improving Canada's productivity, they certainly mean delay, and in some cases permanent delay, in that investment.
As high interest rates wreak havoc throughout the economy, one of the biggest casualties is new job creation. This means higher unemployment at a time when unofficially well in excess of one million Canadians are unemployed. If one is to include in that figure those Canadians identified as being disabled, we are talking about a figure probably touching close to two million unemployed.
It is important to recognize that small business creates two out of every three new jobs in Canada and represents 42 per cent of the employment base, and that by pursuing this policy the government is doing so on the backs of secondary workers in Canada. By secondary workers I mean those workers that are young, old, women, native Canadians, disabled Canadians. These are the people that are first to be laid off, the first to go during an economic crunch. I noted with interest that the president of manpower temporary services, Mr. William Coke, said over the weekend that he would not be surprised to see
May 25, 1981

unemployment easily reach 9 per cent, and I suspect that to be a very conservative estimate.
Also, Mr. Speaker, high interest rates mean sharp increases in small business bankruptcies and the number of firms placed in receivership. Mr. Claude Leduc, the chief statistician for the Canadian Insolvency Association, said the number of business bankruptcies in the first four months of 1981 increased by 17 per cent, with total liabilities up 35 per cent over the same period last year. This indicates very clearly that not only small businesses are being hammered by these high interest rates, but medium and large businesses also are feeling the pinch.
Of course, the official figures on bankruptcy, as bad as they are, cover up the seriousness of the situation. They cover up the impact these high interest rates are having on our economy because for every thousand firms that go through formal bankruptcy, no less than 5,000 firms will finally give up and quietly go out of business or be placed in receivership.
The picture is indeed very bleak but the worst is not over yet, Mr. Speaker. Farmers must be included in our comments on small business. There are over 250,000 farmers operating across Canada, and whether they own a family farm or a corporate farm, it is fair to say that 99 per cent are indeed small businesses. High interest rates in the farm sector raise the cost of just maintaining herds, let alone expanding a cattle or hog operation. High interest rates raise the cost of financing new machinery and equipment as well. This, of course, hurts the thousands of small businesses across the country in our farm communities who sell and service farm machinery.
And what of the bigger businesses that manufacture farm machinery? What of the hundreds of smaller manufacturers that supply this industry with parts and components? Indeed, when one considers the cash flow problems that small farmers are facing and the fact they are unable to expand during this time, it is a sad day for the agriculture sector and for the small farmers in Canada that this government continues with its high interest rate policy, a policy made in the United States and which the government seems to be quite prepared to continue and increase.
Of course, as mortgage rates also climb above the 18 per cent range the housing market is shaken at its very foundations. Young Canadians who have saved and worked hoping one day to purchase their home watch their dreams crumble with each successive increase in mortgage rates. The great majority of construction firms are small businesses again, Mr. Speaker, and there are 88,000 of them across Canada. These are not the Cadillac Fairviews, NuWest or the Bramaleas; they are local firms employing local citizens in our communities and purchasing building materials and supplies from other small businesses.
High interest rates also take their pound of flesh out of the consumer. With finance charges at an all-time record level, consumers are reluctant to purchase new automobiles or new appliances such as refrigerators and ranges. This understandably is having a devastating effect on these industries as well. The Canadian Appliance Manufacturers Association now esti-
Small Business
mates that 4,000 fewer major appliances will be sold in Canada this year than were sold in 1980. But that is just sales, which includes imports. For the domestic industry the outlook is even worse. Major appliance imports as a percentage of the domestic market have risen to nearly 30 per cent from 24 per cent during the period 1975 to 1979. This government's high interest rate policy is guaranteed to accelerate further the decline of our manufacturing industry and slowly strangle thousands of small parts manufacturers dependent upon this industry, not to mention the small retail appliance stores in communities across Canada.
Of course, members of this House are well aware of the plight of Canada's auto industry and auto parts industry and one need not go into detail on this particular major sector of our economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Maybe the Liberals should hear it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Maybe the Liberals should hear it one more time.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but the point I want to make is that this government's high interest rate policy is doing serious damage, both short and long term, to the entire economic fabric of Canada, not only to certain restricted sectors. The small business sector, the automobile industry, the construction industry, the farm sector, appliance manufacturers, first time home buyers, families renewing mortgages, even municipalities that need to borrow in order to make long-term public investments in sewage treatment plants, water systems and recreational facilities which are so important to their communities-nothing is left untouched by this government's high interest rate policy.
And what have we gained? Inflation has gone up since Mr. Bouey started tightening what he calls the money supply. That has obviously been a failure, but the Canadian dollar has more or less stabilized between 83 and 86 cents. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will probably go down in Canada's history books as not being the one million dollar man but the 30 cent man for Canada.
We have heard today, Mr. Speaker, that the government's response to these devastatingly high interest rates is the consideration of introducing a number of schemes, gimmicks, concessions or special deals. This is, of course, in response to the various lobby groups, pressure groups and special interest groups that are attempting to make their point with the Liberal cabinet. In other words, we have high interest rates but not for everyone. With these special arrangements we bring in further inequalities in the Canadian economic system and further disparities in the treatment of various groups.
The best example of this is the small business development bond. This was an idea first introduced by the Tories and brought into being by the Liberal government, which we, of course, supported because we believed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and I am not certain why at this point, when he said it was the government's intention to assist and support small businesses in Canada. We took him at his word, much to our chagrin today.

May 25, 1981
Small Business
As the small business development bond began to take shape, we found that it would not provide much help to the
940.000	small businesses in Canada. There were a number of exclusions built into it. Right off the top, it excluded the
350.000	unincorporated businesses and the hundreds of thousands of small businesses requiring financial assistance in order to provide them with working capital. Other exclusions were the fact that the small business development bond could not be used to recycle equipment; it could not be used to purchase used material, equipment or machinery. The small business development bond does a great deal to create more inequalities in the Canadian economic system. In spite of its good intentions, many inequalities and exclusions are built into it. We really have a small business development bond which assists probably fewer than 5 per cent of the small business community.
Unfortunately this program also provides tax shelter relief to those who need it least. It provides tax shelter relief to the corporate lenders of Canada-they are the main beneficiaries-at a time when their profits are at all-time record levels.
The government should direct the Governor of the Bank of Canada to lower interest rates, in which case we will not need the small business development bond or the number of other schemes to assist small farmers and fishermen. They simply want reduced interest rates so that home owners, for example, can requalify for their mortgages and first time home owners can qualify for mortgages. Therefore, I hope the minister will have something for us, when he stands in the House shortly, which will indicate to the small business community that he is prepared to open up the SBDB to provide an opportunity to unincorporated businesses, farmers and fishermen and which will ensure, perhaps most importantly, that the benefits go to the borrowers, not the lenders.
For a country with the potential of Canada to be a dynamic and innovative leader in the world economy as well as its own, venture capital is much needed. In this respect, the Federal Business Development Bank has failed to provide risk capital or venture capital. It has failed to be a lender of last resort. It has turned out to be one of the most conservative lending institutions in Canada.
The high rate of staff turnovers often results in inadequately experienced loans officers. One could go on and on about the problems associated with the Federal Business Development Bank; they are well known. In many parts of Canada it is looked upon as nothing short of a financial disaster. Rather than encouraging Canadians to dream of a better future, it drags Canadian entrepreneurship down and essentially eliminates the possibility for many Canadians to build a better future for themselves and for Canada.
The FBDB must be totally re-evaluated in terms of its mandate, organization and policies. It should be a model or a leading light for venture capital opportunities for Canadian entrepreneurs. It should be used as a clearing house of information for all federal government programs to assist small businessmen. But it sits and essentially retards the development of Canada. This must be changed and the sooner the better.
The previous speaker mentioned the need for research and development. One cringes when one sees that the government's aim is to obtain 1.5 per cent of the GNP by 1985. The government itself admits that this is possibly a hopeless target. It should be recognized by us all as totally inadequate, because 1.5 per cent of the GNP for research and development will not provide the technological leadership the country drastically needs at this time.
More money and efforts should be expended on federal research institutes and educational institutions. More emphasis should be placed on industry and business to develop a more aggressive policy when it comes to research and development, through to the production stage. Research and development per se is inadequate. The government must set the guidelines or the parameters. It must provide initiative for the private sector to move in the direction the government seeks to develop. I am not certain we need another 50 kinds of underarm deodorant. We need research and development which is guided and makes sense in terms of industrial advantages in Canada and research and development through to the production end. It will create more jobs for Canada. It will provide expertise for Canadians and from Canadians. It will develop a technological leadership for Canadian industry and for the world.
At this point in time we mainly require an active commitment by the government to the small business sector. Earlier today we recognized that the government decided to introduce metrication in the retail sector which will require the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars on measuring devices and scales in order for retailers to comply with the initiative taken by the government. While we support the principle of metrication, we abhor that because of the timing hundreds of millions of dollars of equipment and machinery will have to be sourced from beyond Canada's borders; they will have to be sourced from the United States and abroad. If the government is committed to a buy-Canada policy, if the government is committed to the small business sector, this is where it can provide sound leadership and a strong model to business across the country.
Also the previous speaker mentioned the paperwork burden facing small businessmen. There is no question that this is the case. We must take seriously the matter of the paperwork burden of small businessmen. I spent the last number of days speaking with small businessmen from Kamloops who are good businessmen. They depend upon the state of the economy to develop their sector adequately. They are committed Canadians who want to do a good job. They want to co-operate with government authorities, but now they have reached the stage where they are prepared to say, "We cannot take it any longer".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
May 25, 1981

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) on the motion which he introduced in the House today and which gives us the opportunity to discuss an important sector of our economy, namely Canadian small businesses. I would also like to congratulate him on the contents and the tone of his speech since, as he said in his introductory remarks, we have to rise above partisanship if we really want to serve well the interests of this community which concerns every one of us.
I appreciated particularly his comments concerning regulations and the horror stories which he told us because I also know a few of them. The hon. member can be assured that my colleague from the Treasury Board, who is responsible for the general deregulation on behalf of the Government of Canada and myself, as I am more specifically responsible for reducing paper work for small businesses in Canada, will be very happy, not only to follow his advice, but also to ask him for advice to bring about a situation where regulations will no longer be a constant barrier to entrepreneurship in Canada.
I am also happy to note that he speaks in his motion of the increased need for risk capital to provide additional stimulus and strength to the small business sector. It is obvious that at the present time in spite of the relatively important operations of the Federal Business Development Bank with regard to loans or the placing of risk capital on the market, in fact, no financial institution in Canada entirely meets this need.
However, I would like to mention to the hon. member simply for his information that there are agencies in certain provinces, such as the Small Business Development Corporation in Ontario, SODEC in Quebec and the Venture Capital Corporation in Nova Scotia. My colleague from Alberta also mentioned that he was establishing some type of agency to promote activities or loans for risk capital. There is only one question I would like to ask at this time: I wonder whether or not we need another federal agency in addition to those which now exist in the provinces in this field. I believe that it would be more appropriate to increase co-ordination with provincial agencies to be able to set up one system throughout the country which would make available more risk capital to men and women in business. I must say that I was very pleased with the comments of the hon. member concerning the profits of the business sector, and I agree completely that if we want to continue as a country and as a nation to have some of the most generous social, medical, old-age assistance and unemployment assistance programs to meet the needs of our community, it is essential quite obviously for small businesses in Canada to have the best possible margins of profit.
Like the hon. member for Burlington, I am not afraid of the word profit and I hope that an increasing number of our small
Small Business
businesses will be able to make these profits which they have a right to expect. I am also glad that his motion mentioned the issue of research and development. It is true that our country may not have a sufficient percentage of its revenue invested in research and development compared to other member countries of the OECD, but the government has undertaken to increase this percentage to 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. I hope that, as the years go by and as the financial situation of the government improves, we will be in a position to implement even more generous programs to promote research and development, either through tax measures or other means, to help the promoters establish these research and development programs, and we could perhaps even, as suggested by the hon. member, give a tax credit for the purchases made to set up scientific libraries in business companies, for instance.
I was therefore very pleased with the comments made by the hon. member for Burlington, but unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the same cannot be said about my reaction to the whinings of the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), who recited all he has learned by rote, which he has been repeating these last few months and which is full of untruths and half-truths. He indicated at the very beginning of his intervention that the present policies of the government delay the development plans of small businesses and prevent Canadian small businessmen from purchasing the new equipment they need and from expanding their business to create more jobs.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell him that that was precisely why the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) promoted the small business development bond program in his budget. Under that program, as the hon. member knows, businessmen can borrow at roughly half the current or commercial rate. It is used specifically for business expansion purposes, either for the purchase of real assets, land, buildings or new equipment. So that answers the first objection raised by the hon. member. Then the hon. member said that the policies of this government are leading to higher unemployment rates. Mr. Speaker, he seems to forget, or he is probably not aware of this, that in April we reported the lowest unemployment rate since 1976. Instead of looking at the figures as they are he would rather throw a scare into everybody by saying that the unemployment rate will soar to 9 per cent, 10 per cent and 11 per cent. He wants to scare Canadians.
Then the hon. member went on to a topic so dear to his heart, bankruptcies, saying that they had gone up by 17 per cent in 1980 and during the first quarter of 1981. Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance stated during today's question period, of course the economy suffers from any bankruptcy, but no useful purpose is served in stressing only one figure as did the hon. member who he failed to mention in the same breath that, although bankruptcies may have risen by 17 per cent in 1980 and in the first quarter of 1981, there were 20 per cent more new businesses in 1980 and that same percentage

May 25, 1981
Small Business
holds true for the first quarter of 1981. He also failed to point out that the total number of bankruptcies in the sector of small businesses still represents less than 1 per cent of all small businesses in Canada. And as a universal remedy, of course- this he suggested during the question period, as if he were living on a remote island in mid-Pacific or mid-Atlantic, I could not say-the universal panacea for all such woes he described to us, when he stated that the government only has to lower interest rates. I suggest that it is a rather simplistic view of the components of the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker. Apparently the hon. member does not give a hoot either for the considerable damage done by inflation to the future of small businesses in Canada.
A little further on in his speech the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap again repeated his favourite statement, namely that the Federal Business Development Bank is Canada's most conservative financial institution, that it strangles small businesses, shies away from risks and no longer serves the purposes for which it was created. I should like to tell him very simply that the bank made a study of its lending characteristics, which study reveals that, in 1975, 52 per cent of FBDB loans were fully guaranteed as compared with only 31 per cent in 1980.
Since there were more loans that were not guaranteed, there were naturally more loan calls. In 1976, the reserve for losses included in operating costs was equal to .9 per cent of the total loans outstanding at the FBDB, in 1980, it was equal to 2.4 per cent. I wonder whether the hon. member could name me one commercial bank or "caisse populaire" or credit union which incurs losses of 2.4 per cent on loans to small business. If so, Mr. Speaker, I will agree with him that the Federal Development Bank is too conservative an institution for small business.
The bank's figures and an analysis of its loans show that the hon. member's assertion is unfounded. The hon. member did however make one good suggestion, that is that the Federal Development Bank with its network of 102 offices throughout the country should serve as a distribution center for federal programs. I certainly agree with that, and so do the bank's officials. During the training course that they must take, the bank's credit officers are made aware of all the existing programs that can aid the small business sector, and we try to use this network of 102 offices across the country to distribute information regarding federal programs.
The hon. member went onto talk about his latest pet peeve, metric scales. He thinks, Mr. Speaker, that it will cost hundreds of millions of dollars to replace existing scales by metric scales in grocery stores. That is another red herring, because according to the information I have, replacement costs in food chains and retail grocery stores will amount to between $45 and $58 million. That is a far cry from the hundreds of millions of dollars the hon. member speaks of.
He is shocked, perhaps not without just cause, that we do not at this time have the capability to manufacture such scales in Canada. Since 1976, all Canadians have known that metric scales would be introduced in retail food stores in 1979 and, for various reasons, this was delayed until January, 1982, that is three years later. And yet since 1976, despite all our efforts to encourage investors to go into the manufacture of metric scales, only one Canadian manufacturer, located in Ontario, decided to take up the challenge. We certainly hope that when conversion is implemented in 1982, he will do a booming business. Why did not other Canadian manufacturers go into that venture? Probably, Mr. Speaker, because they considered that the volume of sales, which is some $50 million, was not worth the investment required to go into this new line of production. We are not of the opinion, like members of the NDP, that we should take investors by the hand and tell them: Sir, Madam, would you please manufacture scales. Our programs are well known and so are our policies, and it is not by behaving in the paternalistic fashion suggested by the hon. member that we will develop in Canada a healthier, more aggressive and more dynamic business sector.
We do not deny, Mr. Speaker, that high interest rates affect small business in Canada and that the cost of borrowing money is getting ever higher for small businessmen. However, before considering new programs and setting up new stuctures, let us look at the programs already in place. The hon. member who moved the motion pointed out that the Small Businesses Loans Act has been in force since 1961, and in 1980 alone, it is interesting to note that Canadian small businessmen have borrowed over $400 million, Mr. Speaker, under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
You will remember that less than a year ago, last June, 1 introduced some amendments to that legislation in order to make more people eligible and to raise the maximum amount of loans through a more flexible rate scale providing for larger and easier loans. Loans granted under the Small Businesses Loans Act are 90 per cent state-guaranteed and may be granted to manufacturing concerns, to wholesale and retail firms, to service industries, to building, transportation, communication, real estate businesses as well as to insurance agents and brokers. We are then trying to cover the greatest possible number of small businesses so that they may enjoy state-guaranteed financing.
Secondly, I dealt briefly with the Federal Business Development Bank which, in spite of all its deficiencies and the present difficult economic conditions, plays an essential role in the country in that it is the only institution at present that provides a cheap management consultant service for small businesses. It also provides throughout the country, in our remotest cities, a series of management seminars so that businessmen and businesswomen may acquire new administrative techniques, learn how to improve their bookkeeping and to run their business most efficiently. In addition to the financial role played by the
May 25, 1981

Federal Business Development Bank-someone just said that such a bank has no place in the market-Mr. Speaker, I hasten to point out that the average loan granted by the Federal Business Development Bank is about $49,000. Let us look at the average loan granted by chartered banks. You will see that it is around $500,000 or more. It means that the small business community in Canada is not served by the Federal Business Development Bank. I think it is a gross distortion of the truth. The management consultant services such as the management seminars of the Federal Business Development Bank are a most valuable tool, particularly in remote communities, because up to 1980, the bank held more than 7,000 seminars throughout the country, not in cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary but in more remote communities where customers do not have access to all the government services provided in large cities. In addition to the FBDB and the program under the Small Businesses Loans Act, there is another program, the business development program, which meets partly the needs of small businesses to finance their activities in the area of research and development.
Mr. Speaker, just to give you an idea, I have here an April press release that says that under the industrial development program, during January and February, $42 million were allocated to industrial development projects in Canada as innovation grants for new products, for design, for increased productivity, for the identification of new products and for proposed projects. This program also provides for adjustment assistance in the form of loan guarantees for the reorganization, development and upgrading of equipment, as working capital or contribution to hire consultants to prepare restructur-ating proposals.
Mr. Speaker, that was the business expansion program for February and January. The amount was $42 million. And another news release issued on May 12 showed that for March, an amount of $14,230,215 had been granted to support industrial expansion in Canada. This means, therefore, that there are at this moment programs which provide for and facilitate research and development, help our men and women in business develop new products and find their way, after months and years of effort, into the export markets. And this is exactly how all Canadian corporations, whether small, medium or large, will get a chance to survive. That is the reason why the government has decided to significantly increase both the credits allocated to the export promotion program, and the financial resources of the Export Development Corporation. If 1980 has been a record year as far as exports are concerned, this is due to all the mechanisms we have set up to help businessmen forge ahead in their quest for new markets outside Canada.
Moreover, the National Research Council has its own industrial research assistance program. Under this program, the council contributes approximately 40 per cent of the total costs of research and development carried out by Canadian corpora-
Small Business
tions. The industrial research and development mini-program implemented in 1979 was aimed at providing additional assistance to small businesses. We seek to encourage small businesses in Canada to participate more resolvedly in research and development activities, to develop new products, since we are all too aware that creativity is found mostly in small businesses. It is a fact that in 1980, small businesses were responsible for 62 per cent of the new jobs created in Canada. As a matter of fact, this sector is responsible for 42 per cent of all the jobs in Canada. It is clear that this government, like the other governments before it, is extremely concerned with the welfare of small businesses, just like all provincial governments for that matter. As I was saying earlier, an additional coordinating effort must be made in conjunction with all parties concerned, because as a result of the current fiscal situation, there is no longer any room for competition between the provincial and federal governments to set up programs, because we are all using taxpayers' money.
I suggest that the time has come to accept that when a province decides to support research activities in a particular area, the federal government should avoid getting involved in the same area. I think that we must co-ordinate all federal and provincial policies to help small businesses.
I have referred to the small business development bond program; this assistance, however, is not to be considered as a source of working capital. But I feel that the purpose was to have a special mechanism to favour the growth and development of dynamic small businesses and make it possible for them to purchase any new equipment they need to increase their production. Under item 4 of the small business development bond program, banking and lending institutions may consider using this program to refinance corporations which are facing serious financial difficulties. I think, therefore, that the necessary mechanisms exist to provide assistance in that area.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will remember that some time during the summer, my colleague, the Minister of Supplies and Services (Mr. Blais) and I having told ourselves that the state should serve the small business sector, introduced the subcontracting program. As we know, the federal government is the largest in the country; it spends for goods and services about $4 billion a year. We therefore decided to recommend a subcontracting program providing that for all contracts entered into between the Department of Supply and Services and a supplier, and amounting to $2 million or more, the contractor be required to tender a plan of his subcontracts with small Canadian businesses. Even though at this time about 38 per cent of government purchases in supplies and services, and representing about $ 1 billion, go to small business, we hope, thanks to this subcontracting program, to reach a target of 45 per cent of all central purchasing, precisely to help small and medium-sized businesses.

May 25, 1981
Small Business
In addition to all those programs, as you know Mr. Speaker, there are special tax incentives for small businesses. The main one provides for a lower tax rate on their income. As you are aware, the rate on the first $150,000 earned by a private company under Canadian control is 21 per cent lower than that applying to big business. I know that in all my contacts with the small business community throughout Canada I am often reminded that the amount of $150,000 to which the preferential rate applies has not been changed in four years. I agree that at some time or other that ceiling will have to be raised, when the financial situation of the government allows. Moreover, again in the field of tax measures, let us keep in mind that the carry-over of as much as $200,000 in capital gains in the transfer of small businesses between generations has been proposed. There is also the tax credit on research and development spending by small businesses. Small private Canadian-owned companies that are entitled to the lower tax rate that I mentioned in the first tax measure can also benefit from an investment tax credit of 25 per cent on all their investments in research and development.
There is also the sales tax exemption on manufactured goods of up to $50,000, the tax-free allowance on provincial aid to risk investments such as, for instance, the investments made by the Small Business Ontario Development Corporation, or SODEC, or the Venture Capital Corporation of Nova Scotia. The assistance given by those corporations is tax exempt. The last budget also provides for deduction of the spouse's salary for non-incorporated businesses in Canada, and contains another program I have spoken of at length, the small business development bond.
I now come to the paperwork burden reduction, Mr. Speaker, since I am in charge of that program in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I know that this is one of the most constant and justified concerns of the Canadian small business community. It is figured that the paperwork required by the federal government from the business community, from both large and small businesses in Canada, would each year fill a train stretching from Montreal to Toronto. So this is to say to what extent we are flooded with paperwork, with a multiplicity of forms.
I was a little sorry to hear that the hon. member from the Progressive Conservative party was not aware of what had been achieved by the Paperwork Reduction Bureau, probably because he did not attend my press conferences. I would like to point out to him, for example, that in August of last year I announced a series of 50 measures precisely with a view to reducing the paperwork burden for small businesses in Canada. One of the most important will save about $100 million for the business community because we have limited to six years the retention of business records. Previously, as the hon. member knows, there was no limit, and some businesses kept papers for 50 years -

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

speechtext:
I will come back to that if the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) will allow me to continue. Until last August, the burden of proof lay with businesses. They had to write Department "X", "Y" or "Z" to ask when they would be allowed to destroy those-I was going to say darned papers encumbering their basement, attic and warehouses. The onus is now reversed: We say: "The six-year period is up, you can discard all the old papers". If some departments want businesses to keep records for more than six years, they now have to ask for it and specify why they have to be kept.
So, after six years, businesses no longer need ask permission to destroy their files or records, and the onus is on the department to justify any request for keeping papers going back more than six years. Here is a more practical example: customs and excise regulations were amended and now allow importers to list all their shipments on a single form instead of having to fill out a separate form each time. They remit taxes and charges once a month instead of doing so for every shipment.
Statistics Canada was requested to change a number of inquiries, particularly the monthly inquiry on employment, payrolls and individual hours; it is hoped this will reduce the burden imposed on small businesses, saving them some $35 million. Also, the Department of Labour was requested to review the famous question of the time logbook that every trucker in the country must fill each night.
