speechtext:
I am thankful to hon. members for allowing me to conclude my remarks. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am very grateful to the hon. member for introducing this motion. I would like to indicate to him that I share his concerns in respect of risk capital, the financing of working capital, the red tape and the matter of research and development, and I accept wholeheartedly his offer to co-operate. To sum up, I would like to submit to the hon. member that at this point in time, if we look at the whole range of loans guaranteed under the Small Businesses Loans Act, all the loans from the Federal Business Development Bank, loans guaranteed under the business development program, the Canadian government currently has upwards of $3 billion in guaranteed loans to small businesses as of May, 1981. And if we add to that business development program grants, grants from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, grants from the National Research Council of

May 25, 1981

Canada and other departments, we see that some $100 million in grants are extended to small businesses every year. And finally, as far as fiscal measures are concerned, if all revenues lost in the form of either tax deductions, preferred rates or business expansion bonds were added up, they would amount to $2 billion a year of extra help to small businesses. These in my view are huge investments, but admittedly we still have a long way to go, and 1 count on my colleagues from all sides of the House to help me bring back to a more acceptable level the red tape and regulation burden and create an over-all economic climate that will be more favourable to small business expansion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the minister of state is sincere in his concern for the small business sector. I appreciate his sincerity, but I feel sorry for him. It is obvious that his hands are tied by the more senior cabinet ministers of this administration. They do not share his enthusiasm for small business. If one follows the record of the Trudeau administration, small business has been virtually ignored.
Just over one year ago the Liberal party platform during the election campaign was based on lower inflation, gasoline prices and interest rates. After the Liberals received their mandate presumably to pursue those policies, they instead subjected Canadians to over one year of debate on the Constitution. They virtually ignored the blatant signals of real economic difficulties.
When the constitutional debate left this House a few weeks ago to await the Supreme Court ruling, the first piece of legislation brought forward by the Liberal administration was the youth offenders legislation, followed by the elections act to shorten the period of elections. There has not been anything to deal with economic matters, especially those related to small businessmen. It has only been at the urging of the opposition parties that we have had an opportunity to debate any matters relating to the economy.
During this one-year period of inaction on the economy, gasoline prices increased by 49 cents per gallon and inflation climbed from around 10 per cent to nearly 13 per cent. The biggest culprit damaging the small business sector in Canada has been interest rates, which have now skyrocketed to nearly 20 per cent prime rate. That means small business pays well over that. At the same time, people are losing their homes, business bankruptcies are on the increase and farmers are being forced from the land.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) have the gall to maintain that Canadians are much better off than they were a decade ago. I would like to quote from a letter to the editor in today's "Trudeau Star"-I mean the Toronto Star. I believe it expresses the feelings of the majority of Canadians. I quote:
Regarding the article "No more aid to consumers, Trudeau says," Prime Minister Trudeau's statement to the House of Commons that Canadians' after
Small Business
tax income has risen 50 per cent over the last decade and, therefore, "Canadians are 50 per cent better off, on average, in 1980 than they were in 1970" is asinine.
In 1970 we bought our home with a 10 per cent mortgage. My husband was and still is a municipal worker and I did not work. Our gas cost $10 a week to go to work and I could feed our family for $35 a week. Our property taxes were $250 a year. We managed on one salary.
Ten years later, my husband's salary has increased-averaged over 10 years- approximately 60 per cent. This does sound fantastic!
But it now costs us $30 per week for gas to go back and forth to work-an increase of 200 per cent. The mortgage rate is now 18 per cent, if you're lucky- an 80 per cent increase. It costs us $85 per week for food-another increase of almost 150 per cent and our taxes have more than doubled.
I could go on and on with percentages of price increases, but I think every working Canadian family knows this.
I now have a full time job myself, out of sheer necessity, and then I pick up the paper and read we are 50 per cent better off now than we were 10 years ago.
Garbage!
Trudeau's statement is an insult to my intelligence and the sooner he and Finance Minister Allan MacEachen get down off their high horses and start doing something to get Canada out of this economic mess it's in, the better off all Canadians will be.
I read that into the record because, from talking to my constituents and people across the country, I feel it exemplifies the feelings of Canadians today regarding the inaction of this government. The Minister of Finance says that high interest rates will reduce inflation. That is hogwash. The higher the interest rates, the more a businessman has to spend to finance his company. He will pass along the cost of that increase in his product to the consumer, the consumer will have to pay that much more and that feeds inflation. Economists do not often agree on anything, but they do agree that high interest rates feed inflation.
Government spending continues to rise. Government spending is the main reason for domestically caused inflation. There is no question about that. Last year this government spent an estimated $67.6 billion. Projected costs of services to government increased again this year by $4.7 billion. The Liberal government is spending at the rate of $129,000 per minute, 24 hours a day. It is the inability, ineffectiveness and obvious non-urgency of the Liberal administration which are causing the problems in our economy.
When they were in opposition, the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance condemned the PC government for trying to reduce government spending in the civil service in order to reduce inflation and, therefore, interest rates. During the election campaign, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) promised to resign if interest rates did not go down if and when the Liberals again formed the government. The Liberals again form the government, interest rates have skyrocketed and the minister is still here, he is not resigning. On October 30, 1979, while a member of the loyal opposition, the same minister said:
Because of the harmful effects of high interest rates on consumers, businessmen, especially small businessmen, and the entire economy, there should be an urgent study by the finance committee, where the Governor of the Bank of Canada would come, and the Minister of Finance.
He went on to say to the then finance minister, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie):

May 25, 1981
Small Business
I want to point out to you that your high interest rate policy would slow down the economy, it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs; it will mean increases in the cost of living. It will probably bring the housing and construction industry to a halt, with thousands of jobs being lost in these sectors.
How right he was, Mr. Speaker. Even so, the Progressive Conservative Party went on to meet his challenge by introducing a budget that would have returned purchasing power to the lower and middle-income earners. We were prepared to implement a small business policy that would meet the real needs of the vital sector of our economy. We reduced government spending and provided incentive to business and individuals. We proposed energy tax rebates to lower and middle-income families, an employment tax credit, and a mortgage and property tax reduction for middle and low-income families. We proposed all of these things, yet the government had the gall to tell us that interest was too high when it was below 14 per cent at the time and to defeat a budget which would have reduced interest rates and inflation even more.
What has this government done? It has initiated a debate on the Constitution for a year and has brought forward the young offenders legislation and things of that nature without having the least bit of compassion for the small businessman in this country or, indeed, for the individual across the land. Naturally every Canadian and every sector of the Canadian economy is adversely affected by this lack of action on the part of this insensitive and arrogant Liberal administration.
The one sector that is affected most by this lack of action is the small business community. We have said over and over again that the small business sector of this country is the backbone of our economy. It is the largest potential employing sector in Canada. In fact, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) just stated it employed over 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada last year. This is why the Progressive Conservative Party has moved this motion today, and I should like to take the time to read it into the record once more:
That this House condemns the government for ignoring the consequences of its high interest policy and for its failure to assist the small business sector in Canada
(1)	by increasing and extending the small business development bond program;
(2)	by encouraging venture capital investment by means of appropriate tax adjustments;
(3)	by relieving the small business sector from the massive weight of government regulation; and
(4)	by fostering the research and development necessary to preserve the vitality of Canadian businesses of ail sizes.
I very seldom get angry, but I am getting fed up and very angry about this inaction. I have talked to small businessmen in my constituency and across the country, and they are angry about the inability and the inaction of this government to take the necessary steps to reduce inflation by reducing government spending and bringing down interest rates. It is a cop-out to tie interest rates to the weekly bond issue, as the Prime Minister has done, and therefore absolve himself from the responsibility
for high interest rates. It is a cop-out even to tie them to United States rates. They should not be tied to United States rates. We must accept temporarily lower exchange rates for the Canadian dollar if we untie interest rates from U.S. rates,
I agree, but I believe, as does the majority of businessmen, that we will temporarily have to suffer a tougher exchange on the dollar if we are to bring interest rates down. The government must act on this question.
I feel sorry for the Minister of State for Small Businesses because he is not allowed to act on his own. It is obvious that in dealing with interest rates his hands are tied. He just had an opportunity to take some specific action in reducing interest rates but he could not do so.
The small business development program should be extended beyond 1981. The government did not want to extend it even to the end of this year. It was as a result of urging by my colleagues, myself and others in opposition and across the country that finally the government reluctantly moved to extend the program. It should be extended for another one, two or three years so that businessmen can make long-range plans instead of depending on the ad hoc, band-aid approaches and temporary programs this government has set up.
Perhaps the small business development bond program should be expanded to include venture working capital, because businesses cannot continue to carry inventory, payrolls and day after day production paying over 20 per cent in interest. Small business development bonds do not cover working or venture capital.
Perhaps loans under the small business development bond program should be tax deductible in order to benefit small businesses with profits as well as those which are not in the black. Profit should not be considered a dirty word-something which has resulted from this Liberal administration's policy. Businesses with profits today cannot deduct the interest paid on borrowings made under the small business development bond provisions. Therefore, profits from that bond program are minimal. The rates are nearly parallel to conventional loans.
The Minister of Finance has said from time to time that the government cannot afford to do this. Let me refer very quickly to a study made by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business on the economic impact of the small business development bond. It concluded that there was no net cost to the federal treasury for small business development bonds, but an actual gain of $77 million in the first year of the program. Surely that reduces the validity of the argument of the Minister of Finance that it is too costly a program. He just does not care about small businessmen and the interest rates they are paying today.
Since my time is running out perhaps I could make one final recommendation. I have nothing against profits. As I just said, profit has become a dirty word around this place in recent years, but I think profits tend to create productivity and
May 25, 1981

expansion of businesses. However, during these present circumstances the high bank profits of today should be channelled into loans at preferential rates for small businesses guaranteed by the government. This could be done through the existing Small Loans Act under which the government is already guaranteeing chartered bank loans at prime plus one, I believe it is. The minister of state boasts about the number of loans the government is guaranteeing under this act, but does the guaranteeing of loans at 21 per cent or perhaps 22 per cent help small business? I do not think it does and nor do small businessmen. This preferential rate should be tied to the cost of living or the inflation rate. These are some of the things that should be considered.
Unless immediate action is taken to bring down interest rates in this country, particularly in the small business sector, we will lose this sector as we now know it. It will no longer exist. This country was built through incentives, initiatives and the well-being of small businessmen. This is what we can grow from and build in the future, but what is this government doing? It is reducing small business to a small portion of our economic productivity, because small businesses are now dependent on the government's actions which cause them to suffer 20 per cent interest rates and more on their borrowings.
I do not care if we have to sit here for months on end, but if this Parliament does nothing else it should lower interest rates. The only way to do so is to start by providing preferential interest rates to the small business sector.
In closing, let me say that my colleagues have talked about regulations, directives and controls. These things still exist and they must be replaced by incentives. We must give tax rebates and other incentives to those small businesses which invest in research and development. We should provide an incentive tax credit to any Canadian citizen who makes a direct investment in the equity of a Canadian-owned business. Incentives must replace the many stringent regulations and controls that have been established during the Liberal reign in the last ten years. It is time the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister put small business where it belongs, and that is at the top of their list of priorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third almost consecutive day that the business of the House has given us the opportunity to discuss the issue of high interest rates, and it is unfortunate that some forget to look at the problem in its general context. The opposition condemns the government for ignoring the consequences of high interest rates, as though short-term high interest rates did not result in the long run into a decrease in inflation and consequently in interest rates.

May 25, 1981
Small Business
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, we were able to explain last week in what context the current high interest rates in Canada had to be considered during the debate on the motion introduced by the New Democratic Party which suggested that interest rates in Canada were being set outside the country. We saw how economic conditions caused inflationary pressures and expectations, how these pressures resulted in certain monetary and fiscal policies which brought about higher interest rates, and how, if we wanted to have an effective policy against inflation, we had to suffer in the short term the unfortunate effects of certain measures so as to meet this medium and long-term objective of fighting against inflation.
What I find surprising is that after the motion of the New Democratic Party, a motion for the Progressive Conservative party was introduced by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). He blamed, of course, the government for its high interest rates, and singled out as one of the causes the very large government deficit and the unlimited expenditures of the central government.
Mr. Speaker, the members opposite, especially on the side of the Progressive Conservatives, should make up their mind and decide whether we should reduce the deficit as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has undertaken to do and is now doing, or else they should say unequivocally that they do not believe in reducing the deficit, and do what the hon. member has done today and ask the government to increase its expenditures and extend the program of small business development bonds. The hon. member who has just spoken told us, on the basis of solid Social Crediter arithmetic, that this measure would cost the government nothing. He said that it would cost nothing and would even bring revenue to the government. He would have to prove it, and he has not done so yet. However, it is a well-known fact that a tax credit allows a business to deduct from its payable tax part of the interest due on its loan and also allows a lending institution to deduct from its revenue that part of the interest it will not collect. One has to calculate like a Social Crediter to suggest that it does not cost the government a thing because revenues not collected by the government are losses, and a tax expenditure, whether it is a taxation or a budgetary item, is an expenditure all the same.
I want to believe in authoritative arguments, but in arithmetic as in taxation, such arguments are inconclusive. Even if Mr. Y said that a tax expenditure does not cost anything, we can very well believe him, but let us ask him to explain how a tax expenditure does not cost anything to the government.
When amendments to the Income Tax Act were considered-if I am not mistaken, it was in early February-several members in all corners of the House, especially the Minister of State for Small Businesses, urged the government to extend the small business development loan. We remember that the Minister of Finance had rightly and reluctantly agreed to extend for another year the small business development loan. He did it for two reasons: first, because of the economic
circumstances, high interest rates being prejudicial to the development of small business, and second-keep in mind that we were then still in a recession-in order to promote economic development. Small and medium-sized highly job-oriented businesses would be in a position to make further investments in order to give a new economic impetus.
The minister responsible told us a while ago how the government, with that small business development bond, with others institutions under his jurisdiction and with other government programs especially under the aegis of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, promotes the development of small business and enables it not only to get through the difficult times we are now experiencing but to develop further in spite of those difficult times.
There was also some reference to tax measures designed to encourage small business risk capital. As for that particular aspect of risk capital, I should like to point out that the government has taken several steps to ensure the development of small businesses in a sound and favourable climate. Obviously, the measure I have just spoken of is of great importance to the development of small businesses, but we also have tax measures that are of great benefit to them. All privately-owned Canadian businesses enjoy a major income tax concession. The federal income tax rate that applies to them is 15.75 per cent as compared with the normal 37.8 per cent applied to big companies, or compared with the income tax rate that applies to foreign-controlled companies. In other words, the tax rate applied to small Canadian-owned companies, that is, 15.75 per cent, is roughly about half that applied to foreign-owned companies. So, when I am asked to provide special tax measures for risk capital, I say that having an income tax rate of barely half that normally applied to companies is clearly an advantageous tax measure, and it already exists, Mr. Speaker.
In the case of the profits of Canadian manufacturing and processing firms, the rate applied to small businesses is even lower than the privileged rate of 15.75 per cent I have been discussing; it stands at 10.5 per cent compared to the current rate of 31.5 per cent applied to unincorporated businesses. That substantially lower rate is clearly of special advantage to small Canadian business; it also represents an important federal government tax measure aimed at encouraging risk capital investment in small and medium-sized businesses. That type of tax expenditure in terms of lower tax rates amounts to about $1 billion in revenue losses for the Canadian treasury for the year 1979.
Research and development has also been mentioned, Mr. Speaker. In the field of taxation we also have an extremely important measure concerning research and development: a 25 per cent tax credit for investment in research and development in the case of expenses incurred by Canadian small businesses. A 25 per cent tax credit has to be a rather generous measure. Other tax measures are aimed at supporting provincial programs covering venture capital investment. There is also a
May 25, 1981

refundable 25 per cent tax exemption on investment dividends when the investor company is eligible as a venture capital company under certain provincial programs.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, we are being urged to come up with special tax measures designed to promote research and development as well as venture capital investment, and it has been shown that our tax system already features measures applicable to any of the measures which the opposition is calling for.
Above all I would like to insist on the fact that three of the four suggestions made in the motion openly call for government expenditures. And yet, last week, the same Progressive Conservative party asked the government to reduce its deficit and its expenditures. Cut down your spending! Cut down the public deficit! But at the same time, hardly one day later, they forget everything they asked for and say: boost expenditures by extending the small business development bond program and by encouraging venture capital investment through tax measures. Where is the logic in that? It is the logic of the illogical Conservative policies. Now either you believe in the cutback approach or you do not. But if you do not, then you have to be consistent and stop behaving like a weathercock changing your views from day to day in an effort to gain some of the popularity that has been escaping you for some years now, and I am talking about the Progressive Conservatives.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) dealt eloquently with the third item, since he is responsible for lessening the burden of regulation and red tape which weighs down Canadian business. It is his responsibility and he is supported in his efforts by the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), and I certainly hope that with their combined efforts they will be able to lighten the burden of regulation and red tape which small business must now contend with.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to recall that the aim of this government is to fight against inflation so that in the short and mid-term, with a more balanced economy and improved economic health, Canadians will be better off. By trying to relieve some sectors, either temporarily by subsidies, or directly, or by tax deductions, we would only be destroying with the left hand what the right hand is trying to do as a matter of policy, that is to lessen inflationary pressures so as to have lower interest rates resulting from a more stable economy.
That was the basis and the outline of the budget the Minister of Finance introduced last October. I for one am convinced that if we pursue with determination this policy of reducing the federal deficit, of controlling expenditures, and of implementing a gradualist monetary policy, we will in the mid-term achieve a more stable economy, lower interest rates and a lower inflation rate.
Small Business

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate today on a matter which I am sure is of extreme importance to all Canadians. In following the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) I think there are several comments that are appropriate, particularly to the references he has made both to the small business development bond and in terms of the government's monetary policy.
Perhaps one of the handicaps he has in looking at this is the advice of the same people who have been guiding the economic policy of the government for some years now, but I would like to refer him to a comment made May 20 in The Globe and Mail which was attributed to Walter Gordon, a previous minister of finance. Mr. Gordon, who was chairman of the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy, said at a press conference that the current high interest rate policy is fuelling, not fighting, inflation. The bank's present course has itself been a part of the problem rather than part of the solution.
The minister has just said that you get four different economists and four different policies. I suppose that is true. Perhaps it makes the objective assessment of what should really be done difficult, but at the very least it should bring into question the type of policy the government is following at the present time. Some of the other comments that have been made-and there have been many things written about this lately-would suggest indeed that the options of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) are limited to the point where he is waiting to see what will happen with inactivity on his part. Indeed, as we recess for the summer the government will have an opportunity to remove itself from some of the pressure coming from a number of areas and different interest groups in the country that are feeling specific pressure for specific reasons, most of which are not of their own making.
As an example-and this stems from one of the comments of the minister in the Flouse today-it is very difficult to believe he is not aware of what is going on in the country. He seemed to suggest that he did not believe that farmers were in more difficulty, that people were actually having to walk away from homes, that small businesses were experiencing increased bankruptcies.
I think the first thing that has to happen if there is to be any movement in this whole area is that the government must recognize the problem, but in light of the kind of comments that the Minister of Finance has been making it appears that he does not recognize the problem. 1 would extend to him an invitation, as I am sure most members on both sides of the House would, to go out into the country and talk to people; not just those who have experienced bankruptcies, but people who are forced to leave their businesses or who decide they can no longer hang in there.
I can tell the minister that in one area alone where I made an effort to draw up some statistics we are facing a situation where on a year over year basis we will have nearly five times the number of people who may not face the spectre of bank-

May 25, 1981
Small Business
ruptcy but who will be forced, because of a change in their equity position in terms of their debt load, to get out of the business they are in, whether it be agriculture or otherwise. The number of farms for sale, particularly in my area, is expected to be 300 per cent higher this year than last year simply because of the economic climate the government is fostering now.
Also in his comments, the minister suggested that the reduction of the federal deficit was one of the prime efforts of the government. If we look at the deficit position of the government in the last year, it seems to me we are actually looking at an increase of $4 billion over what was projected in the Crosbie budget. I do not want to compare two different budgets, but in terms of looking at this as a mechanism for lowering inflation, 1 do not know from where the minister gets his figures. I have heard this several times in the House, but every time I look at the figures I realize they do not agree with his comments. Perhaps he would at some time try to bring me up to date on what kind of figures he is drawing from.
In this year alone government expenditures have risen to approximately $62 billion and the deficit is up to $14 billion. They are clearly giant increases in each area. It portends even worse for the future. In 1983, 1984 and 1985 we will be looking at yearly government expenditures somewhere near $90 billion. This is not in agreement with the kinds of things the minister has said.
I should like to comment briefly on what he said concerning the small business development bond. A previous speaker on this side of the House suggested that if the small business development bond were expanded, it would allow business to take advantage of lower interest rates. This would help them increase their activities and avoid bankruptcy. The minister suggested that it was costing the government a lot of money and that the presentation which has been made was not accurate.
Because there are a number of different economic theories from different economists, I think it is reasonable to quote one economist who suggested very strongly that we would benefit from this type of move because of the activity it would generate in the economy and, in the long run, tax dollars would be generated; this would return funds to the government. I think this is the idea of the hon. member. Certainly it suggests that the minister should rethink his position and perhaps take a look at a fresh viewpoint, rather that sticking with the same kind of attitude that has been adopted hitherto.
In a recent book entitled "How Ottawa Spends Your Tax * Dollars", Bruce Doern noted that the Liberals have abandoned social priorities of the Pearson era and that a prime example is its failure to cushion lower-income groups from the effects of higher oil and gas prices as in the 1979 Crosbie tax credit.
In the perspective of economic distress under which we are now, I suggest very strongly that we are not dealing with the social aspects of what we are supposed to be doing or what I suggest we should try to do. The difference between lower and
upper-income people and the number of people below the poverty line is increasing, not decreasing. We are not accomplishing the transfer of benefits to lower income groups, although it is suggested that we are doing all these things economically on behalf of the nation at large.
Much has been said about the government's interest rate policy, its impact on small business, and the way in which it is addressed. The Canadian Institute for Economic Policy indicated that small and medium-sized business, most of which are Canadian-owned, are borrowing heavily from the banks for their capital requirements. Many of these businesses have been driven into bankruptcy; they are in situations where they have no recourse but to go into bankruptcy.
Perhaps it is a sad commentary that one of the major bills before the House of Commons now is the bankruptcy bill. A bill addressing economic issues rather than bankruptcies would give a more favourable light to what are the activities and priorities of government. The number of bankruptcies in March, 1981 was 29 per cent higher than a year ago according to the figures of the institute. We heard a number of figures today, including 17 per cent and 18 per cent. Whatever it is, it is a significant amount. As was mentioned, even that amount does not address the entire problem because it does not indicate the number of people who are voluntarily withdrawing from business rather than face full bankruptcy.
There has been mention of the automobile industry. One of the more interesting and important viewpoints on this subject came recently from the United States and was published in the Atlantic Monthly. It drew a comparison between the automobile industry in North America and the automobile industry in Japan. Although we are addressing small business, I mention this becaause of the differentiation between small business and large business. Whether it is a large energy project or whatever the megaprojects will be, whether in fact it is agriculture versus small business, most come down to some common denominators. Certainly one major common denominator is the cost of borrowing money in order to do business.
The automobile industry in North America is experiencing severe distress. In the last year alone, Ford experienced a massive deficit of approximately $1.5 billion and Chrysler had losses of $1.7 billion. The market share of the North American industry has decreased significantly as Japanese models have come on stream.
There are many factors in this area. Many Canadians who have bought foreign cars tell us about their quality and the terrific relationship between Japanese workers and their parent organizations, as well as a number of other things.
The research and development aspect is perhaps one of the most important, but we should consider the amount of capital reinvested in research and development, the manner in which products are brought on stream and organized, as well as the entire series of marketing and other manoeuvres. The research and development aspect is one in which Canada in particular is vulnerable, as many people know, in a number of ways. It is vulnerable in the immediate sense in that we have not been able to maintain the competitive aspects either at the research
May 25, 1981

and development level or at the fully developed and commercialization phase. This speaks to the co-ordinating activity of the government as a prime mover in research and development. Regardless of its dedication to providing a certain percentage of the gross national product, allowing certain programs, a tax credit system or whatever mechanism it chooses, something has been lacking.
There are specific examples in a number of areas. However, the government has been lacking in the management aspect of the whole scene. This management aspect must be improved in terms of providing a relationship and a linkage between universities, government and business itself, particularly small business. Small business does not really have the facilities or the resources to develop products or do basic research on things which would be in their best interest, such as their product lines or things they would like to be innovative in. This was the consistent finding across Canada at all provincial government levels with which I had the opportunity to have discussions. It is something which has not been addressed meaningfully in the activities I have seen occurring or in government programming.
As the government looks at a five-year program in research and development, it is still treading lightly and very hesitantly in terms of adopting a full program. This is precisely the point. The management aspect of it requires a long-range view. It requires a consistency in funding and in programming. Indeed, it requires an understanding of the required management capabilities in order to be effective.
In a broader sense, I think the Canadian nuclear industry has been faced with the same thing. I mention that as an example since there is a recent reference to it which I think should be read by many people who are interested in this area. I am speaking about the Secor report which addresses Canada's situation in terms of the development of its research and the international aspect of what is quickly becoming a high cost and high technology area. The Candu reactor is a prime example of this.
There are many other areas which we will be developing, but the Secor report breaks down these so-called high cost and high technology areas into three or four major points. The report suggests that these areas have common factors in the global market and that the systems must really be sold across international boundaries in order to maintain a viable industry. The report states that these systems should be competitive in an international sense, that is, competing with other people in other countries at all times and continuing to do so. The competition must be won if these industries are to survive.
[DOT] <1720)
Finally, it is mentioned that there should be a technology push, that it is necessary and important to maintain technology investment and to keep up with changes in a technological way in terms of refinements which will allow industry to maintain whatever market share they have. These are matters which have never before been addressed in Canada. It does not appear as though they will be addressed in Canada.
Small Business
I think the whole system suffers simply because we do not have the management or involvement that we will need if we are to keep up with international competition and if we want this high technology to survive. One of the major points which I think must be made is that if we do not choose to do this, or if we are unable to achieve it, whilst remaining competitive- unless we go the route of continual subsidies-then we will put ourselves back into a state where we are only able to provide raw resources. It is as simple as that. We do not have a great number of options from which to choose. We must face the international marketplace and its requirements. This issue must be faced in a meaningful way, not just in terms of one big industry but in terms of the peripheral activities which take place and which cause our economy to function.
I draw attention to the tar sands projects. The Financial Post has suggested that one of the few short-term hopes we have is in the area of tar sands development and heavy oil projects, that if we do not get them off the ground with the investment they require and do not realize the economic activity they will generate for small industries across the country, we will be out of luck in three or four years.
I think it was interesting to hear the minister of state suggest that with the programs the government has in place now we will not be out of trouble any sooner than three or four years. That is a comment made by another economist, not by myself. He says it will take that long to achieve the effect we want-at least three or four years before we will achieve the desired result. I do not think we can wait that long. 1 know that a great many small businesses and industries involved in agriculture simply will not survive unless there is some shortterm redress to the problem which they are facing today.
One other point I would like to mention with regard to research and development which the government has missed to date is with regard to equipment. We could take a great deal of time to talk about what kind of training we must have. However, the limited time allotted to me at this juncture does not allow for that. There has been an additional assessment of the kinds of equipment our universities have and what is happening to our basic research and development programs at that level.
A task force which reported during the last few months has found that we are about ten years behind-most of our equipment is at about the ten-year vintage. While that speaks well for the maintainers of our technological equipment, it has put us out of the race in a great many high technology areas. We have been left behind because of the rapid change in equipment and the ability to maintain a competitive position is just not there. We have old equipment which will require a massive amount of investment in order to upgrade it. This task force report is available through the National Science and Engineering Research Council of Canada and I think would be worth while for many people to look at.
The Science Council report states in part:
Complex scientific, technological and economic problems of the future cannot be met by using second rate institutions to generate new concepts and to train the manpower required.

May 25, 1981
Small Business
Several times the priorities of the government have been mentioned and what has been done in the last year or so. I have a list before me of the government's priorities. At the top of the list, as we all know, is the Constitution, which has really taken a great deal of our energy. It is still very much unresolved and is a matter which still has to be addressed.
Returning to the list, the budget follows the Constitution in terms of priority. The number of budgetary measures which actually address the short-term economic problems which we face have been very few indeed. Next on the list come the National Energy Program, the western Canada strategy and a review of major social policy arrangements.
What has really been lacking is a sense of urgency with regard to making the economy the first priority. Until the government admits that the country is having difficulties we will not attain the appropriate priority this situation demands. We will continue to meet the foil of matters like the Constitution, matters of social policy and the like, which are not really addressing the real short-term needs of Canadians.
There are many things which can be said, but 1 feel that the major emphasis as far as research and development is concerned is that we must have a government which is sensitive, not just to simple funding, but to the entire concept of managing these programs. Co-operation among our universities, small businessmen and governments must be encouraged if we are to facilitate the basis for economic recovery in our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege this afternoon to assess for the edification of members of this House the relationships that this administration has established and can be expected to promote between the federal government, research and development and the business community.
I would like to open my remarks by insisting that, the criticisms of the opposition notwithstanding, this government places a high priority on fostering research and development in industry, assisting companies of all sizes to increase their growth and profitability through the performance of R and D and by applying new technologies to their operations.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) announced the federal government's intention to foster an increase in national R and D expenditures to 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1985. Within this over-all target, it is proposed that the federal government's expenditures should rise from .4 per cent of GNP to .5 per cent, that industry shares should rise from .4 per cent to .75 per cent and that the balance of .25 per cent should be financed by the provinces, the universities and others.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the largest increases in research and development will be required in the industrial sector, and the federal government intends to continue to place
a high priority on assisting Canadian companies to undertake profitable research and development activities. It is equally clear, as most hon. members already know, that the major role will have to be played by the industrial companies themselves, but I hasten to add they will be greatly assisted by a business environment in which innovative activities are strongly encouraged.
The federal government has long recognized the importance of supporting research and development activities, and has therefore introduced a range of incentive programs and taxation incentives which, I believe it is fair to say, are among the most generous in the world. For example, very substantial financial assistance has been given to companies such as Pratt & Whitney, de Havilland, Canadair, and Bombardier, as well as many others in the high technology sectors of Canadian industry.
To focus on an area of particular importance, I would direct the attention of the House to the federal government's announcement of April, 1979, which initiated a special electronics program to introduce the secondary industry in Canada to the benefits of using microelectronics in their manufacturing processes and product design. The first part of this program consists of grants for major projects in all sectors of the manufacturing industry. Two very substantial grants have already been made under this section of the program, one to Mitel, and the other to Sentrol. However, it would be wrong to give the impression that only large companies in the electronics area can gain from this program. A number of smaller companies have applied-in the food, textiles, metals processing, and other industrial sectors-and grants have been approved for monitoring of diesel engines for small fishing vessels, pantyhose manufacturing, and control systems for bakery operations, while others are expected to be approved in the near future.
A second part of this program will promote the awareness of Canadian companies of the importance of applying microelectronics technology to their operations. In considering the role of technology, we must recognize the importance of the application of technology to industrial processes, in order to make the processes more productive and competitive. It is not only the supply of high technology products to world markets which is important-it is absolutely vital that we increase the productivity of all our manufacturing and processing operations if we are to prosper, or, perhaps, even to survive, in the future. So, I can assure the House that the federal government intends to play its role in order to ensure that Canadian companies are aware of the importance of the application of technology.
A large proportion of financial assistance in support of R and D has gone to the larger companies, for the simple reason that their research and development operations are much larger than those of smaller companies. Nevertheless, a substantial amount of assistance has been provided to smaller companies. Departments of the federal government, including the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, have regional
May 25, 1981

offices in all parts of the country for the purpose of ensuring that assistance from the federal government is as effective as possible.
A large number of smaller companies have also been assisted through a variety of institutions which have been established under programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am pleased to say that over $23 million have been invested in the establishment of 27 of these institutions, which provide research and development, testing and technical training services to industry in a variety of industrial sectors and in all regions of Canada.
It is well known that small companies have a difficult time in commercializing technology and starting up new companies, especially those which involve inventions and technical ideas. To provide such assistance to small companies, and even private individuals, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has financed the start-up of two industrial innovation centres, one located at the University of Waterloo and the other at Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has a number of other programs to support industrial R and D. First, there is the Enterprise Development Program which will normally support 75 per cent of the direct costs of product and process development projects and market and productivity improvement studies. This program is administered, in the main, by the regional offices of DITC in the ten provinces in order that its application and use will be closely based on the needs of the various regions of Canada. Because of the criteria used in project selection, this program has been of particular assistance to small and medium-sized business.
Total spending under the program in 1980-81 was about $38 million, and it is estimated that approximately $2.0 billion of product sales will result over a period of five years.
The equivalent of the EDP program for those industries- primarily electronics and aerospace that are in the business of providing high technology military equipment for export market requirements-is the Defence Industry Productivity, DIP, Program. Under this program the federal government shares the cost of product developments related to export military markets as well as the costs of acquisition of modern production equipment. D1PP spending for the 1980-81 fiscal year is about $120 million and is expected to rise to over $150 million in 1981-82.
The National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program, IRAP, and the Program Industry Laboratory Project, P1LP, are other government vehicles for promoting and supporting industrial research and development in industry. Under these programs, financial support is provided for selected industrial research projects of good potential. During the period from April, 1962, to March 31, 1981, IRAP supported 1,313 projects from 655 companies for a total contribution of $183 million. It is estimated that each dollar of funding produced $20 of sales on average. IRAP's budget for 1981-82 will be about $29.4 million of which some $2 million will be directed towards companies with less that 100 employees. Approximately 400 projects from industry
Small Business
have been supported under the PILP program since its inception in 1975 for a total contribution of about $40 million. Is is expected some $12 million will be spent in the 1981-82 fiscal year.
In addition to these specific programs, the federal government has adopted a contracting-out policy for its own R and D requirements. The objective is to increase Canadian industry's R and D and innovative capability. Under this policy, federal government departments must contract out their R and D requirements to the private sector, except in those instances where there are compelling reasons for the work to be done in government laboratories themselves. In 1980-81 approximately $139 million was spent under 2,500 individual contracts.
In the important field of energy, the federal government is currently contributing some $15 million to the private sector for R and D work in renewable forms of energy-such as solar and biomass-and in energy conservation in industrial processes. In addition, $3 million is being provided for research on improved methods of extracting crude oil from tar sands and heavy oil deposits and in coal gasification and liquefaction.
In total, the federal government contributed some $264 million in grants and contracts to industry in 1980-81 for industrially initiated R and D. That figure is expected to increase to well over $300 million in 1981-82.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that I have provided this House with convincing evidence of the federal government's resolve to assist companies of all sizes to develop a technological capability, to perform R and D which will assist them to meet the challenges which Canada must face in domestic and international markets, and to apply new technology to their processes so that they can remain competitive and productive in the face of international competition. I realize, of course, that government programs are not the whole story, by a long shot. Canadian industry must share its burden of the responsibility to remain innovative and competitive as I am sure it will, and thus ensure a sustained economic growth in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak on this motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling).
Each morning as I walk to my office I find myself pausing frequently to enjoy the beauty of the Parliament Buildings and surrounding grounds. Inevitably my eyes are drawn to the top of the Peace Tower. There, night and day in all seasons, is the flag of this great nation at once both a symbol and a commitment, a symbol of a land of freedom and opportunity; a commitment that the people of this land will keep it ever so.
But today as I looked at that flag, I was struck with the contrast evident between potential and reality. It came to mind that, given the record of this government, the flag should have been flying upside down. It should be flying upside down, not as a gesture of disrespect but in compliance with the international code of distress. This country is not only in distress, it is

May 25, 1981
Small Business
in severe distress. This country is in serious condition, and a great many of us are well aware of it. And because of the calculated indifference of this government, things seem to be getting worse. There is no doubt that everything else is upside down, so why not the flag? Is the government waiting perhaps until the economic chaos it has created gets so bad that it will simply then hoist the white flag of surrender? A good many of us feel the government should do that already.
The government is forcing thousands of Canadians to surrender. Every day that passes, more and more Canadians have to surrender their homes, their farms, their businesses and their jobs. Pretty soon we will all be waving white flags because there will be nothing more to surrender. There are others on this side of the House who have repeatedly and urgently tried to get the government to take responsible action to eliminate the mess we are now in. They have spoken of the plight of thousands of Canadians. They have dealt with the general situation and with particular segments. I join in condemning this government and wish to draw attention to a particular community in this country which is among those most hard hit by this government's economic mismanagement.
1 am speaking of the thousands and thousands of small businessmen in all provinces and in every sector of this country.
This government has subjected the small business community to a number of financially punishing burdens. The relentless push to metric conversion is a perfect example of this. Converting to the metric system has been a monetary nightmare for the business community and consequently the consumer.
Conversion in the retail food sector, forcing grocers to switch meat and produce scales from ounces and pounds to grams and kilograms, could cost us as much as $200 million. I noted the comments of the New Democratic critic, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). 1 also noted the comments of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) who seemed to raise his eyebrows at that amount, implying he thought it was a ridiculous figure. I believe he quoted conversion costs as amounting to between $45,000 and $48,000. I presume he meant that $45,000 to $48,000 would apply to certain individual stores. He is shaking his head. But I am quite sure that for Eaton's, Simpsons, and the Bay the cost of conversion will be a lot higher than $50,000. It was mentioned earlier by other speakers that the majority of the metric scales will have to be purchased abroad which, in turn, will provide jobs outside of the country instead of here in Canada. This relentless target date of January 1, 1982, is certainly unpopular.
One grocer in a metric conversion test area said that he had to pay $900 to convert his scale, and the test cost him $100,000 in lost sales when customers went elsewhere.
An overwhelming majority of businessmen and consumers are opposed to metric conversion. But this government has never shown the slightest inclination or willingness to respond to public opinion, and there is no indication that it ever will. The devastating impact of the fiscal ineptitude of this government is quickly and painfully destroying hundreds of small
businesses in this country every day. Because the small businessman and businesswoman live in the shadow of the giant corporations, the impact is harder for many to recognize.
There are over one million small businesses in Canada and they create two thirds of the jobs. Small businesses in this country generate at least 20 per cent of the value of all goods and services produced. The small business community is obviously a vital segment in our economy, a very important constituency that cannot and should not be treated in an offhand manner.
1 am sure that the minister for small businesses understands this. I would suggest to him though that he ensure that his own aides realize it as well. It was disturbing to learn that a call to his office last week to obtain figures on the small businesses which I have just cited resulted in a reply that the office kept no such figures, and the suggestion was made that the caller try elsewhere. Surely the credibility of a minister is in question when people in the minister's own office plead ignorance when asked the most basic of questions. I heard the minister today give some indication as to the importance of small business. If people in his own office do not seem to have this information, I would suggest that he have his aides read his speech carefully so they will have it. If small businesses were to operate in the same manner as some of the people in the minister's office, they would soon be out of business. One would think, given the reams and reams of paperwork forced on small businesses by the government, that statistics would be crowding the minister right out of his office.
For years the small business community has been inundated with mandatory government forms. Some businessmen and women spend about as much time on government paper work as they do in operating their own businesses. This pile of paper, completed under duress, is both annoying and costly. It is frequently unnecessary. The small businessman and woman, not having the resources to hire high-priced lawyers or accountants like their multinational counterparts, must shoulder the paper work burden alone. A good many of them burn the midnight oil in order to complete these many forms. Some of the paper work these days involves government bankruptcy forms.
There are more bankruptcies in small businesses than in any other segment of the economy. We heard statistics and figures given showing just how many bankruptcies there are at the present time. Thanks to the government's acceptance of the policy of higher and higher interest rates, many small businesses have gone under, and there are reportedly hundreds more which are on the verge of bankruptcy.
Just this past weekend I spoke to two or three of the businessmen in my community. One in particular, a hardware merchant, mentioned the high interest rate he was paying on loans, I believe it was 21 per cent. This is a staggering amount. It is also a reason why so many small businesses are in such serious condition.
People all across the country, who have worked hard enough to save money to start their own businesses and who have put in long hours to make sure their business remains viable, are
May 25, 1981

now losing everything. Many of them mortgaged their own homes as collateral to help their businesses get started or to expand and are, therefore, in a position now where they may even be losing their own homes.
When small businesses fail, the owners of those businesses are not the only ones affected. Their businesses, collectively, employ millions of people. In fact, the majority of working men and women in this country work for small firms, not for large corporations and not for government. Therefore, when a business goes bankrupt, the unemployment level rises. When hundreds of businesses go under, thousands of people lose their jobs. This tragic situation did not occur overnight. On the contrary, things have been getting progressively worse for months. When members on this side of the House were requesting urgent and immediate action on economic issues, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had more important matters. The Prime Minister had his Constitution and his charter of rights and, to him, these were of prime importance. We are well aware they took up the time of the House of Commons for months. They were concluded only recently, having been sent to the Supreme Court.
A place in the history of the nation will be valueless if the nation itself is destroyed. With the constitutional issue now before the Supreme Court, the Prime Minister wants to reassure the nation that the economy is headed in the right direction. To demonstrate that he is taking things seriously, he has spoken of holding a federal-provincial meeting on economic issues. If such a meeting is held, the climate of consensus would hardly be achieved.
How could the provincial premiers be expected to consult, exchange views and attempt to resolve problems with the very man who, during the constitutional debate, treated them with ridicule and contempt; much the same sort of contempt he and his government obviously have for the small business community. This government neither understands nor has compassion for the problems facing the owners of small businesses. The Prime Minister and members of his government have demonstrated they are oblivious to the problem. The only problem they seem to acknowledge is that people are angry and complaining.
The government does not know why people are upset. We are told time and time again that all is well, that the universe is unfolding as it should. Well, I have news for this government. The universe, for thousands of Canadians is coming apart at the seams. The threads of the economy of this nation are unravelling at an alarming rate.
The growing number of bankruptcies should indicate to this government that something is seriously wrong, wrong with its policies and wrong with its attitude. That hundreds of small businesses have gone bankrupt, and hundreds of others are on the verge of bankruptcy should be a source of alarm for this government.
Let me illustrate for members of this House the reason why even a single bankruptcy can result in a potentially horrendous
Small Business
domino effect. Let us take a small tourist operation, of which there are many in my constituency. The resort, faced with exorbitant interest rates, cannot afford to seek financial assistance for its summer operation. Without sufficient funds to cover the purchase of supplies and salaries for the initial startup, the tourist resort has to close. Cooks, waitresses, the cleaning staff, office staff and handymen are suddenly unemployed. The owner and employees now have no extra money with which to purchase goods and services in the community.
Other small businesses in the community immediately begin to feel the pinch. With fewer people to supply, the owners of these other firms soon have to lay off staff, and the list of the unemployed grows. The tourists who have in the past stayed at the resort now look for other facilities, and again business in the community suffers. Again other people are out of work. Some of those out of work will move to other centres in the hope of securing employment, but others, for a variety of circumstances, will be forced to apply for unemployment insurance or accept welfare. Then, because of one business closing, the community and the country is faced with the prospect of higher taxes to support those whose only resort is the social benefit programs. Everyone's disposable income takes a slight plunge, and the vicious cycle is about to be repeated on other levels.
What I have described is only a small part of the sad circumstances of a single bankruptcy. When you have several small firms going under, the effects on the community and the country are calamitous. How then in heaven's name can this government sit back and do nothing, tell us all is well, when what is happening now is affecting us all?
We cannot afford to lose one of our small businesses, but there are some whose loss to the nation will create more hardship than others. 1 am thinking now in particular of the small farmer. In these days of automation and plastic wrapped meat and produce, there are those who speak fondly of the farming of yesterday. Like sideshow attractions, historic villages offer glimpses of the disappearing communities of yore and display what are now considered quaint methods of production and commerce. Today's farm is indeed often automated, but today's farmer, trying to run his business, cannot cope with the rising interest rates and an absence of economic planning, and he too is going under.
When thousands of small farmers go bankrupt, or lose their farms through bank foreclosure, who will feed this nation? The farmer can be classified as a small businessman. When the price reaches even higher levels than those we have today, who will be able to afford to buy what is available? With so many businesses closing down, will there be anything left to buy?
Mention was made of the small business development bond which was introduced by the Clark government and adopted by the present government, for which they are to be commended. However, it is restrictive in the sense that it is only available to incorporated companies. I hope that because of pressure from all parties, including government backbenchers, the government will consider making it available to individuals and partnerships and continue it beyond the present deadline

May 25, 1981
Order Paper Questions
of December 31 next. It should be a law on the books, and it should continue.
Rather than being restrictive, the government would do well to enlarge the bond so that it provides working capital. Also, it should be available for used machinery and equipment. This would provide much needed assistance to the small businessman. As well, the farmers could take advantage of it.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) took exception with one statement coming from this side. It was said that this would not cost anything. The minister said it was costing X number of dollars. However, if the small business development bond helps businesses to stay in operation, pay salaries, make purchases and sell their goods, as the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) stated, then in the long run the government will end up making money. It cannot be classed as an excessive cost when everything is weighed in the balance.
This government knows all about bankruptcy. In fact this government would have been bankrupt long ago had it not been for its taxing power which enables it to spend into eternity. It cannot go bankrupt. It just prints more money. The government has been bankrupt in thought and deed for some time. It has been said that misery loves company. Therefore, the government seems determined it will not be alone in its mess. The problem is that it is not. It is astonishing to hear the government say that high interest rates are not causing the problem.
