speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was an admirably brief statement from the hon. member opposite. However, we have heard some rather longer statements today, which to my mind indicates how little some hon. members opposite appreciate what has been happening in the area of government support for the small business sector. The opposition motion might have been relevant 30 years ago, 20 years ago or perhaps even ten years ago, but today the motion seems to reflect the curiously anachronistic character of the party which sponsored it.
In any event, let us start at the beginning, because evidently hon. members opposite need information about what the national government is doing in terms of support and incentive for the growth of small business in Canada.
Back in 1976, some five years ago, this government appointed Canada's first minister of state for small business. Since then our efforts to assist small business have proliferated to the point where one of the outstanding, and occasionally justified, complaints of small businessmen was that they have been unable to find their way through the various programs offered by both the federal and provincial governments.
Accordingly, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, through its regional offices located in every province and territory, and its unique small business secretariat, has maintained continuous contact with the small business community. Instant telephone service is available at all times to provide small businessmen with the information they require about the variety of services available. Of course, I want to emphasize that in addition to those services provided by the public service, members of Parliament, at least from this side of the House, have their doors open on all occasions to small businessmen seeking assistance.
It is obviously impossible in the short time allocated this evening to review all the efforts made by the national government to assist the growth of that essential sector of our economy, the small business sector; efforts which, I might note, have won the praise of chambers of commerce, boards of trade, and indeed of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. However, since there seems to be some confusion in the minds of the members opposite about those programs, I wish to note a few highlights.
Some members may recall, for example, that we have introduced income tax measures which benefit small businesses by about $2 billion annually. Secondly, we have responded to the requests of individual entrepreneurs and business associations by reducing the amount of the paper burden that has proven increasingly bothersome to business over the past decades. Resultant savings amount now to something over $300 million annually. I only wish that some provincial governments had been equally imaginative and also had reduced that time-consuming demand facing the small businessman. We have greatly increased the opportunities for Canadian suppliers, especially small businesses, to obtain government contracts, often working nationally with provincial governments to achieve maximum benefit. Incidentally, for small businessmen with complaints about paperwork, red tape, excessive government regulation, or indeed any other problem, we have created a small business advocacy office within the small business secretariat.
Government help first becomes available, Mr. Speaker, when an entrepreneur is starting or contemplates expanding his existing operation. In such circumstances, his main concern is to obtain sound financing. Although the commercial banks necessarily remain the principal source of capital, some firms have continued to encounter difficulty in obtaining funds from them. However, these firms have access to the Federal Business Development Bank, an expanding corporation owned by the people of Canada which now has more than 100 branches across the country. Although the bank assists businesses of every size and variety, emphasis is placed on helping small business. In fact, of the 165,000 loans granted by the bank in 1979, over 90 per cent were for $100,000 or less, with the average loan being only about $50,000, obviously in response to the particular needs of small business. Customers of the FBDB may borrow in order to acquire land or to improve their buildings or equipment, to strengthen their working capital, or indeed to establish a new business. The point I wish to make in referring to the activities of the FBDB is simply that venture capital is available and indeed has been available in increasing amounts for some time. Not including the much larger level of direct loans now amounting to some $840 million to over
40,000	customers across Canada, the bank has recently embarked upon direct equity investment. This now amounts to some $25 million, which is in effect invested in the dreams and aspirations of Canadian entrepreneurs.
I should also briefly mention that the bank extends other services to businessmen, for example, the important services of counselling which are often provided by retired experts from the business community, and management training and investment services are available from the bank. Opposition members will, I hope, join with government members in referring their constituents interested in small business assistance to the local branch of the bank.
Another instance, Mr. Speaker, where government has encouraged venture capital development is through the Canada Development Corporation. The CDC has an important subsidiary which unfortunately is not generally recognized, called Canada Ventures. It in turn has significant holdings in several of Canada's major venture capital compa-
May 25, 1981

nies. Yet another source of financial assistance is provided by the Small Businesses Loans Act under which the government guarantees loans mades by commercial banks and other private sector financial institutions to assist small business to start up and to expand. 1 would note that last year this government raised the ceiling on such loans to $100,000. With the guarantee provided by this act, commercial banks, for example, are encouraged to make loans to small businesses which they might otherwise consider too risky. 1 might also note that last year the bank expanded its capacity by increasing the total amount that may be advanced from some $200 million to $475 million.
I have only sketched in outline, Mr. Speaker, the degree and variety of federal small business assistance. Once a small business has been established, however, there are a number of federal tax measures geared to promote and foster its growth. Let me mention one or two of the more important. Small business tax deductions substantially reduce the impact of federal taxes. What is the effect? Obviously the cash flow of the business improves substantially; there can be no question that the small business thereby gains in terms of its ability to reinvest, to expand and indeed to have a diminished need for financing from outside sources. Our government also extends assistance to small business for capital losses, which differs substantially from that afforded larger corporations. Small business investors are permitted unlimited deduction of their eligible capital losses from their income, a great advantage not available to larger enterprises.
Federal money, Mr. Speaker, is available to help small businesses improve their energy technology, a subject very much in the minds of Canadians today. We are working through the small business secretariat and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to improve the efficiency of energy use in small businesses. We have recently announced our intention to widen the extent of that commitment. Financial support is, for example, offered for research and demonstration projects to ensure that there is greater energy conservation in industrial processes. I might mention that only a fortnight or so ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) opened in Winnipeg the new headquarters of Canartech, the Crown corporation created to promote renewable energy technology. That technology is to be developed, through the use of small businesses in particular to promote small businesses engaged in the provision of renewable energy. I do not doubt that we shall see that Crown corporation grow into one of the most imaginative and effective catalysts for small business development.
Another source of federal assistance upon which I would like to touch for a moment with regard to energy management and conservation is a program that, when applied by industry, has substantially reduced energy consumption in the industrial processes, bringing spectacular savings for small businessmen as well as larger corporations that can reduce their expenditures for fuel and electricity.
Small Business
The fourth part of the opposition motion before us touches on the question of federal government support for research and development. The first three parts of the opposition motion pertain particularly to small business. The fourth part alleges that the federal government has been laggard in providing support for all types of business in the area of research and development. However, I would ask the mover of the motion and other hon. members opposite to note that only recently the business community widely welcomed the announcement that our government intends to raise the national research and development expenditure to 1.5 per cent of Canada's gross national product four years from now, in 1985.
The government itself will contribute about one third of this targeted figure, but in total it represents a co-operative effort with the private sector. Small businesses which have a particularly important part to play in entrepreneurship and in innovative technology, offer some of the best prospects for growth in research and development.
To that end, the federal government will spend about $200 million more this year than last year on research and development so as to move us toward the attainment of our national target of 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. Obviously a part of those funds will be channelled toward university research and development, some will go to government programs themselves, but a substantial proportion will go to co-operative programs with industry. We have already seen emerging in the private sector a concentration of R and D resources on space, communications and energy technology. But I have no doubt that in those areas the support of the federal government has been warmly welcomed and that the support will continue and expand in the future.
Also there are tax incentives available to companies engaged in research and development. Only 100 companies took advantage of those tax incentives as recently as 1977. But the following year the number ballooned to almost 500. That growth has continued, giving substance to the claim that the program is obviously taking effect.
I could continue about the work of the federal government in the area of research and development which the hon. member opposite seems to ignore or of which he is unaware. I want to note that fiscal incentives in the form of tax credits and accelerated write-offs have already had a substantial impact. The second area of concern is the general support programs of the federal government. Further recent initiatives indicate that funds are generally available for financing any sound project, irrespective of the industry sector in which it happens to fall. In that connection, small business support is particularly in the minds of those administering the program.
Also I want to draw attention to the government's policy of contracting out research and development which can have a major benefit on the growth and diversification of activities on the part of companies engaged in high technology areas.
I want to draw attention also to the industrial R and D available through a growing number of programs announced in recent months, programs which were virtually unknown only a few years ago. For example, the enterprise development pro-
9892

May 25, 1981
Small Business
gram has a special fund for microelectronics. In the area of energy, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Ministry of State for Small Businesses have a co-operative program in research. The Department of Communications recently had a major program which led to the development of Telidon, one of the more promising successes of Canadian technology in recent years.
I draw the attention of hon. members to the programs in aerospace which not only involve a significant number of major corporations, but also contribute substantially to the growing competence of a number of small enterprises. All these programs, of which the hon. member opposite seems either to be unaware or whose real importance he does not evaluate, require funds, of course. It seems to me idle for some members opposite to call for substantial reductions in government spending and at the same time to advocate expanded activities on the part of government to finance research and development and incentives for the growth of small business in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the debate this evening on the motion before us, and particularly to deal with the importance of research and development. It must play an important part in the development of a viable and strong small business sector in Canada today.
There is no doubt that various reports, very often commissioned by the government opposite, and various commissions, have shown the importance research and development can play in terms of creating jobs, increased productivity and increased exports, and helping with our balance of payments.
For example, Mr. Pocock, a researcher for the Lamontagne Commission on Research and Development stated:
if Canada had had a GERD of 1.5 per cent in 1978 and assuming 85 per cent of the increase would have been an increase in R&D by industry, there would have been an extra 10,600 jobs for scientists and engineers, which would have also resulted in a total of 1.52 million extra jobs created in new industrial activity and an extra $15.54 billion in exports.
It is amazing when government planners opposite look at ways and means to reduce unemployment and our adverse balance of payments that they do not listen and do not remember the recommendations and words of their own thinkers, their own commissions or their own inquiries. We know that sometimes the Liberals enjoy appointing royal commissions. They enjoy receiving reports and commissioning studies; but not very often do we see the government acting on its own recommendations and findings. Do I need to say that the benefits of increasing research and development would result in increased employment, greater output, greater productivity, improved competitiveness by Canadian industry and businessmen and, indeed, lower prices?
Since I am the critic for science and technology of the New Democratic Party and since I faithfully attend all of the committee meetings, I have learned a great deal. For example, I learned of the Industrial Research Assistance Program of the National Research Council. The NRC conducted an analysis of its program for the years 1973 to 1977. It took the 400 industrial projects represented by 250 companies and the IRAP invested some $93 million of public money which was matched dollar for dollar by private industry. These were the results of the analysis. The investment of some $93 million of private money resulted in a $1.8 billion return to the industries. In other words, it was a return of one dollar for every dollar. The government coffers were increased by some $350 million in taxes which were collected as a result of this investment.
The previous speaker from the government side indicated that the opposition was crying for fewer government expenditures. In some ways we are. I agree in some ways with the Conservative members to my right who say that there can be some trimming in the government's activities. Expenditures in the research and development field are not expenditures, they are an investment. It is an investment which will yield a return of greater tax dollars, of greater economic activity and employment. It is an investment in the country and in its human resources. The IRAP program is but one example of the success which direct investment in research and development can give to the country as a whole. There are several modifications to the IRAP program. For example, there is the mini-IRAP program which is especially geared to smaller industries. What this particular type of program does is to give access to the business community to the biggest resource and the greatest scientific knowledge in this country, that is, public knowledge and public research in the field of science and technology.
The goal of increasing our research and development to 1.5 per cent of our gross national product is certainly not a new goal. I believe it was in 1968 that we heard the government opposite suggesting this goal. It was repeated in 1972 by the Lamontagne commission. In fact, that commission suggested,
I understand, that up to 2 per cent of our gross national product should go to research and development. So, the government must understand that when it trots out with a new goal of 1.5 per cent for 1985, the Canadian public and the opposition remain a little sceptical. Our position is to wait and see.
Finally, I hope that the government is serious about increasing research and development in this country and that we will see some action. In some ways the jury is still out. Definitely, some of the five year plans proposed by such funding agencies as the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council have not been met. For example, the NSERC funding has not reached the level which the five-year plan projected for the second year-it is still below. The government has still not given it's commitment to these research organizations.
We are finding that the universities, which are essential if we are to have the trained personnel to fulfil our objectives,
May 25, 1981

are afraid. They are afraid that they will see a continuing decline in funding. Young university students are not completing their doctorate programs; they are not even commencing their master's programs because there is no assurance that there will be jobs for them. There is a general feeling of insecurity in the scientific community as to what the commitment of this government is and what the future will be. This will affect the business community as well.
One of the major reasons why we have very low expenditures in research and development in Canada compared to other developed countries is to be found in our economic and business structure. Our expenditure is roughly on par with what Portugal and Ireland spend on research and development. Why is this? The major reason is that private industry has not contributed to research and development activities as it has in other countries.
1 would like to read into the record the OECD international comparisons for R and D funding shares as a percentile for 1977 in various countries. For example, in Denmark industry contributed 51.3 per cent, in Finland it was 55.3 per cent, in France 41.1 per cent, in Germany 55.6 per cent, in Japan 65.8 per cent, in Norway 40.8 per cent, in Sweden 59.3 per cent and in the U.S.A. 43.9 per cent. In Canada the percentage is 35.8 per cent-dismally low. It is not small Canadian industry that is to blame. Canadian industry invests in research and development roughly on par with other countries. The fault is that much of the Canadian economy is controlled by multinational firms; and these firms, for a variety of reasons, prefer to do their research outside Canada. One of the two main reasons is that multinational firms have access to high technology from the parent company. Since we are a branch plant economy, there is no reason for them to do their research in the branch plant. This flow of technology across the border has hindered the development of a viable research and development community in Canada. This is the central problem which the government must tackle if we are to achieve our goal of 1.5 per cent. There is no indication that the government is willing or capable of tackling this essential problem. It is not that it does not know about it. The Science Council of Canada have pointed out in various reports the basic structural problem which exists in Canada and which prevents us from achieving our stated goal.
There are no solutions coming from this government. In fact, the slide continues, the slide that we saw during the 1970s when there was a decrease in the expenditures on research and development. We in the New Democratic Party believe that science and the development which flows from it, for example new technology, can and should be used as an important instrument by which Canadians can achieve a great measure of control over their destiny. We believe that R and D should rate a higher priority. It should have an essential priority in the development of any industrial, economic and social strategy for Canada.
We do not believe that throwing money into research and development is a solution. In the past, this government has spent huge sums of money on R and D from which multina-
Small Business
tional oil companies have benefited greatly. Technologies have been developed to which the Canadian public has no access but for which it has paid. This is not an appropriate type of research and development that we would talk about. We suggest that in Canada we agree with what the National Research Council of Canada presented in its five-year plan entitled "The Urgent Investment". I would like to quote three sentences from that report;
Because of Canada's comparatively low population and its unique geographical distribution, a large portion of Canada's manufactured goods is produced in relatively low volume. The technology introduced here must have the flexibility to reduce the inefficiencies found in traditional low volume production techniques.
The National Research Council in its five-year plan refers briefly to the appropriate technologies which we should develop in Canada because they are appropriate to us as a country. I mentioned before that we in this party believe that research and development must play an important part if we are to gain a measure of control over our destinies. It is not enough for us as a country to react to technological innovations all over the globe. It is not enough for us as a society to continually react. Surely we must begin to be in control of events. That is why we feel that the public has an important part to play in developing proper research strategies.
It is also important for us to develop the appropriate technologies. Very often these are not heavily capital intensive but are those that allow local self-sufficiency to develop and a move away from the large, capital intensive, centrally and globally controlled production toward greater decentralization and self-sufficiency.
I feel that this direction is very appropriate for our country, Mr. Speaker. It is an opportunity for Canada to make a significant contribution to the development of Third World countries in particular. It is also an area very appropriate for small Canadian businesses. It would strengthen small Canadian businesses immeasurably. Instead of technologies that require heavy capital funding that depend on the international capital markets, that depend on technologies whose patents are controlled and owned outside our borders, we would, should, and could, develop technologies appropriate to the small-scale production which is suited to our population and which would allow greater participation by small businesses. It would also be more labour intensive.
In the last few decades, small businesses have been wiped out all over the world and markets are controlled by larger and larger firms. High interest rates are but a continuation of this. The economic policies of this government and, in fact, the former Conservative government, and the attitude toward research and development, have all helped to engender a greater concentration on and control over the productive forces.
We suggest that there is a way out, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, research into the appropriate technologies for energy, food production and all the other basic human needs, would make this country into a new, more contemporary country-a coun-

May 25, 1981
Small Business
try which has a great deal of control over its destiny. It would allow this country to have the self-sufficiency and freedom that it does not have at present.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that much of what my colleagues in the Conservative party suggested today makes sense, particularly when they spoke of the neglect of research and development in this country. I hope the government is taking note of the presentations made in the various committees about the need to develop some clear plans for the future that would allow a strong and viable research community to grow in this country, that would benefit small business, the workers and the farmers, and that would make Canada a stronger country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to discuss various important and pressing issues facing Canadians and small business today as a result of the government's economic mismanagement and high interest rate policies.
We have a federal government that has done so little for so many for so long, at the same time as it has done so much to so many for so long. The government has become insensitive and uncaring about the plight of the average and low-income Canadian.
The farm and small business sector along with the consumer and home owner are suffering from the record interest rates that are in place today. To say that the interest rate is high is an understatement; soaring in the clouds is more like it. The government has been soaring high in the clouds for some time without sufficient oxygen to induce clear thinking. Interest rates have taken off like the space shuttle, but with one big difference-the space shuttle came back to earth. The government is taking us on a one-way trip-straight up. I suppose it could use the slogan, "Lost in Space" for its next campaign instead of some of its past logos, such as "The Land is Strong".
The land was strong and it can be strong again, but not under the spell and the rule of the federal government. Inflation, unemployment, interest rates and an energy policy are all important issues, and they need to be solved with leadership and initiative coming from the federal government. Industry needs long-term planning to be effective and competitive in a competitive world. We see countries with few resources become successful world trading nations. The reasons are government support, long-range planning and faith and belief in the country and in the people and, most important, pride in the future.
In Canada we have an abundance of raw materials, knowhow and human resources. Many other countries that have done so much with so little must wonder what on earth Canadians need in order to develop their potential. The government should come out of orbit and down to earth and provide some ground control and ground rules for our future.
I have spoken in the House about the need for a comprehensive industrial strategy for Canada, and made specific reference to the textile and clothing industry in particular and the need to ensure that this industry survives and grows. I have stressed the need for the government to ensure that Canadian industry grows for the future so that we do not become dangerously dependent on a wide range of imports.
In its latest report, the textile and clothing board recommended that bilateral agreements and quotas should be extended to cover the period ending December 31, 1990. I supported the industry's position in asking the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the government to announce the decision on the board's report no later than March 31, 1981, so that business could look with more certainty and support to the future and get on with needed investment and growth.
The industry is still waiting for the government's decision, Mr. Speaker. It is not asking for handouts, but rather for guidance and direction so that it can effectively plan for the future.
The government should realize how important effective planning can be. It lets industry as well as the consumer feel confident about tomorrow and the day after. Planning offers incentives for advancement and the confidence to pursue this. It gets people stirred up in a constructive way. Idleness becomes eagerness, as Canadians are restored to working hard for that great concept of Canada.
Investors need confidence to make the large-scale commitments necessary today. Farming is very big business, even though it could be classified as small business. Start-up costs are extremely high, taking into account necessary machinery and land purchases. The textile and clothing industry requires large capital outlays as well. Such long-range expenditures require future security, and this in turn requires government support through an effective industrial strategy.
The government must combine this with effective emphasis on fostering research and development. This is the key to the future. We cannot sit around on our hands or our laurels and expect to compete or prosper. We can see examples of this in such cases as the British and Japanese automobile industries.
For years Britain had a thriving automobile industry. Then we saw the results of the Japanese introduction of intensive research and development. The British automobile industry was hard hit. We must ensure that our industries do not suffer the same fate.
Research and development and adequate technical training should be high on the government's list of priorities. The success of small and large business in the future requires a co-ordinated effort combined with a comprehensive industrial strategy. This is a big job but it is not insurmountable. Other countries have done it and so can we.
The government must realize the serious state of our economy and must direct its energies to priority issues. Let us tackle the bread and butter issues of inflation, unemployment and high interest rates, and then many of the other concerns will be
May 25, 1981

mitigated. If theories are not working, then the government must take some initiative and act, not sit back and watch the country slide down the rungs of the economic ladder.
Gross economic mismanagement and throwaway overspending have left Canada with a huge deficit and unhealthy interest payments. The government needs a plan to reduce the deficit in the hope of trying to get Canada back on its feet. While in opposition, the Liberals condemned the government of the day for high bank interest rates of some 14 per cent. On January 12, 1980, in Toronto the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said the following:
We have an economic program for the 1980s which will enhance dignity, create opportunity, and provide security.
Since the Liberals took office, the bank rate has risen from 14 per cent to a record 19.06 per cent, as recently announced. The government says it can do nothing about this sorry trend. The truth is that the government cannot be bothered to do anything for the people of Canada who are being so burdened by present economic developments. For many Canadians their universe, instead of unfolding as it should, is closing around them.
The present economic policy of the federal government is a nightmare for small business, for home owners renewing mortgages and for farmers. High interest rates are said to slow down borrowing and spending in an effort to curb inflation. This might have some validity for needless expenditures or certain luxuries, but it is not fair for the Canadian home owner who has to renew his mortgage. This is not a frivolous expenditure, although in light of present government policy it certainly looks more like a luxury when it should, in effect, be a right.
The home owner has already borrowed this money to buy his house and is striving to pay off such a loan. This is not a deliberate new expenditure with new borrowed money to fuel inflation. Yet the home owner is forced to renew this existing debt at greatly increased interest costs in order to maintain the home in which he and his family live.
The government should realize the seriousness and unfairness of this situation and bring in some positive measure to aid home owners facing such high interest increases. We need action now.
Canada is its people and Canada's health and welfare depends on that of its people. How can a country be strong when its economic backbone, comprising small business and the farming industry, are scrambling to make ends meet instead of planning with certainty for the future? The answer is that it cannot. Government cannot sit back and wait for the bubble to burst. The nation, its industry, business and people, need action now. Confidence in the marketplace is essential for planning and future growth.
The present government promised to hold the line on government spending growth to under the rate of the Gross National Product and yet we see spending growth in fiscal year 1980-1981 at 15.2 per cent, compared to the nominal GNP growth of 10.7 per cent.
Small Business
The annual federal deficit is at a high $14 billion, and we pay over $ 11 billion a year on interest payments alone. These factors, along with borrowing on the foreign markets, are fuelling inflation. The federal government wants Canadians to show restraint and help combat inflation. Canadians would like the federal government to set an example and show some restraint and responsibility to commence and maintain the fight against inflation.
The average Canadian citizen is reeling from the current economic situation before us today. Their standard of living appears to be decreasing despite their efforts to get ahead. And yet, at the same time there is a $51 million increase in expenditures on the correctional service of Canada. This must seem hard to understand for the average law-abiding citizen who works to better himself in society. Perhaps such an amount of money would have been better spent if directed toward some mortgage assistance fund for home owners or to fund a program to aid small business and farmers in difficulty during these difficult times.
We have seen how the uncertainties of the National Energy Program have caused havoc in the oil and gas industry in Canada. This affects businesses both large and small. The government's Canadianization of the industry is at huge cost to the taxpayer while not ensuring one new drop of oil. Drilling exploration and capital expenditures are down substantially because of this program, along with a significant decrease in jobs in the industry. This slowdown is felt across Canada in the operations that supply the industry.
Energy supplies and costs are a significant aspect of the cost of doing business to both small business and large-scale business. Again, it is hard for business to plan and to budget when there exists so much uncertainty in the market today. We have been faced with a multitude of energy increases since the last federal election. Relations with the producing provinces have suffered because of the National Energy Program and the Constitution, both imposed on Canadians by the present government. All this leads to uncertainty in the marketplace.
The government is not setting the proper framework to produce the confidence and enthusiasm for investors and business to expand. This framework is needed now so that we can rebuild our economy, fight inflation and unemployment and return to the lifestyle Canadians used to enjoy. We have the potential, and what we need now is leadership and confidence which all together can snowball into a dynamic future for Canada. Concrete measures need to be taken.
While in power, the Progressive Conservative government introduced the small business development bond when interest rates started to climb. This was done in an effort to bring relief to incorporated small businesses. The measure was adopted by the present government and passed by the House in February of this year. After pressure from the Progressive Conservative party along with the business community, the small business development bond was extended to the end of 1981 for qualified borrowers.
This measure has been of great help to small businesses, especially in light of the escalating interest rates. The bond is

May 25, 1981
Small Business
helping to instil some growth in the economy by providing the vehicle to provide the capital needed to carry out plans for the expansion and renovation of businesses.
The government should look at the possibility of extending this measure to unincorporated businesses so that more farmers and small businesses could benefit.
Small business in general needs some relief from the crippling interest rates at which many of them are forced to borrow money. Programs, such as the small business development bond, are useful as positive government measures designed to support Canadian business.
Let us build up Canadian business with pride and give it the support it deserves. These small businesses and farm operations are run by our friends, neighbours and constituents, all fellow Canadians. They contribute to our lifestyle and our economic cycle. When their businesses are strong and growing we all benefit.
We must keep Canadian money in Canada to help Canadians. It does not make much sense to me to pay foreign countries, such as Mexico, millions and millions of dollars for oil when at the same time we pay fellow Canadians much less for a superior product produced at home. That money leaves Canada, much of it forever. Our borrowing on the foreign market has run up an unhealthy deficit which the government seems unable to control. Money that should be used for a variety of constructive measures goes just to try to pay the interest charges on the government's deficit. This adds to the inflation cycle. It is not a good way to run a business, let alone a country.
Canada has the potential to be great, and I think the people realize this. Government can co-exist with business in a free enterprise system without the aspect of socializing everything. There are many options open to a conscientious and responsible government willing to implement realistic long-term solutions for the good of the country. This can be done without stifling business with regulation upon regulation. A prime example of this is the metric madness before us today.
Therefore, I ask the government to come down to earth because that is where the people of Canada are living and trying to cope. A far-reaching and comprehensive industrial policy to allow business to plan for the future is needed to provide a stimulus for growth. Interest rates must be brought under control so that businesses can move ahead, not go under. Programs, such as the small business development bond, should be explored and made available to those businesses who need assistance before it is too late. Canadians want to be able to pay their mortgages while, at the same time, enjoying life, not mortgaging it away.
The government has much work ahead of it. It must build a strong foundation and attack the roots of our economic problems. Inflation must be brought under control and steadily reduced. The present administration has spent years getting Canada into its present condition with irresponsible spending and short-term inconsistencies. I would not be surprised if the government tried to reintroduce wage and price controls after
they had taken us even further down the road. The government cannot patch up its past mistakes with cosmetic measures. They put us into this economic mess and their meddling will only make things worse.
The people of Canada deserve better treatment and realistic long-term solutions, such as those proposed by the Clark Conservative government and the new U.S. administration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this evening. While listening to the speakers this afternoon and this evening, I could not help thinking that perhaps they have overlooked a great deal that has been brought in by this government.
This afternoon we heard mention of the introduction of wages paid to spouses as a business expense. The rate of taxation on small businesses is lower as compared to larger corporations; it is 15.75 per cent. This lower rate is a clear advantage for small Canadian-owned businesses.
Some members feel we are not doing enough research and development. We have a 25 per cent tax credit for- research and development. This measure is designed to encourage venture capital and more Canadian research and development here in this country.
The small business development bond issue was spoken about this afternoon, as well as the Small Businesses Loans Act and amendments to the Federal Business Development Bank. The Federal Business Development Bank is one of the few lending institutions in this period of time in Canada which lends at a fixed interest rate that is renewable or renegotiable after three years.
We heard about the retail scale conversion program to metric which is estimated to cost between $45 million and $50 million. The government provides assistance with regard to retail scales of less than 100 kilograms. Remission of duty is available on imported conversion parts. Such parts are exempt from federal sales tax and are written off as an expense for business. A few days ago we heard indications that none of these are manufactured in Canada. They are manufactured in Canada, one of the plants being in Toronto.
I welcome this opportunity given me today to speak, for example, about the reduction of the paper burden that cuts the paper work required. This government initiative provides for the retention of records for only six years and allows for the submitting of customs and excise documents on a monthly basis. This is a very important move on behalf of the government to assist the small business person.
I would like to elaborate briefly on four major initiatives taken by four different groups pursuing a common goal, namely the alleviation of the paper burden and regulation on the small business community.
In February, 1978, the then minister of state for small business was charged with the responsibility of creating a
May 25, 1981

small business focal point in government, of finding solutions to specific paper burden problems, as well as of identifying long-term methods to alleviate this problem.
After listening to the small business community's complaints, suggestions and requests, after consulting and negotiating with the various departments, the present Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) was in a position to put forward to cabinet a series of recommendations to reduce the paper burden stemming from government forms, reports and surveys, record-keeping requirements and unnecessarily complex regulations and procedures; the two major irritants to small businesses.
These specific measures, developed in co-operation with most government departments, resulted in annual savings to business of at least $300 million per year. These results would not have been achieved without everyone's co-operation in the public and private sectors.
The effort to reduce the paper burden in Canada is a very good example of the kind of action that can be undertaken successfully. Through this activity, however, it was confirmed that the paper burden was only a symptom of, and a direct result from, unnecessarily complex regulations and procedures.
Simultaneously, the federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, decided to attack the whole matter of economic regulations. At the meetings of first ministers on February 13-15, 1978, the following was agreed:
That the whole matter of economic regulations at all levels of government should be referred to the Economic Council of Canada for recommendations for action, in consultation with the provinces and the private sector.
The interim report of the council was produced in November, 1979. It contained procedural recommendations t( increase the accountability of government agencies. The report stressed the need for better consultation procedures with affected groups prior to the introduction of new regulatory initiatives through assessments of the costs and benefits of new regulations. This final report, which will be presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government on June 11, 1981, will propose a system for better management of government decisions about economic regulations. It will feature three major components: First, advance notice and consultation; second, prior assessment; and third, periodic evaluation of existing regulatory programs. The efforts of the Economic Council will certainly serve as a catalyst for assessing the existing myriad of regulations and regulatory agencies.
This House also played a very active role in minimizing the regulatory burden on the private sector. A special House committee was formed to make recommendations on regulatory reform. Individuals, groups, provincial governments as well as officials from a variety of federal departments and agencies contributed to the effort of this committee.
The report released on December 19, 1980, contained 29 recommendations aimed at reaching three primary objectives: first, to improve the process whereby new regulations are drafted; second, to re-evaluate the effectiveness of existing regulations on a regular basis; third, to enhance the accounta-
Small Business
bility of regulation-making bodies to cabinet and to Parliament.
This special committee, among many excellent recommendations, stressed the early consultation aspect with the private sector, including the small business community in the following terms:
The key to more effective regulation involving the least possible burden on the private sector is the participation of a wide variety of interests in the process of regulation from the earliest possible stage.
While this committee found widespread support for regulatory reform from the public and private sectors, it did not obtain the same total support for "deregulation". However, we are positive that, in some instances, deregulation will result from the implementation of some of the committee's recommendations. This initiative will create major benefits for the small business sector.
Another example that proves the government's commitment to regulatory reform and, by the way, to help the small business sector, is the fact that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) has been assigned by the Prime Minister the responsibility to oversee and co-ordinate the government's regulatory reform efforts. I understand that good progress is being made in the elimination of unused, ineffective and undesirable laws and that a bill to this effect will be introduced very shortly.
Another activity that retains the attention of the small business sector is the one related to the guidelines for standardizing and, in some cases, reducing the periods of time for which the federal records must be retained by the business community. An interdepartmental committee, under the chairmanship of the co-ordinator, regulatory reform, is actively involved in the work, with the participation of all departments which administer statutes requiring the private sector to keep records. Ten other major projects now fall under the responsibility of that committee, projects which should have a greater impact on the small business community.
In my remarks today, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to show factually the serious commitment of the government toward reducing the paper burden and the regulations required of the small business community. These different approaches reflect the wisdom of the government in recognizing the fact that any effort to reduce the paper burden and the regulations must not compromise the needed flow of information. We all want regulatory reform. Great care and thought is needed to design the changes required. I believe the government is on the right track in this area of great importance to the private sector. The small business community is looking to this House for leadership and guidance in the matter of regulations and paper burden. Certainly we cannot and will not disappoint this important group. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss this most important motion presented by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling). I should like to read

May 25, 1981
Small Business
it into the record once again because of its importance. It states:
That this House condemns the government for ignoring the consequences of its high interest policy and for its failure to assist the small business sector in Canada
(1)	by increasing and extending the small business development bond program;
(2)	by encouraging venture capital investment by means of appropriate tax adjustments;
(3)	by relieving the small business sector from the massive weight of government regulation; and
(4)	by fostering the research and development necessary to preserve the vitality of Canadian businesses of all sizes.
I should like to discuss just a couple of things relating to this motion. My colleagues have addressed most of the matters, but let me deal first with the high interest rate policy of this government. 1 do not think there is anyone here who would deny that the high interest rate policy is ruining many individuals, many business people and many farmers in Canada. It is particularly hard on senior citizens and people on fixed incomes.
We have a prime rate in Canada of 19.5 per cent, but most people cannot borrow at that rate. That rate is only for the most credit-worthy customers of the chartered banks. Most people who borrow must borrow at commercial rates of around 20 per cent, 21 per cent or 22 per cent. Those who owe money through credit card use, pay anywhere from 24 per cent to 30 per cent, and those who borrow from finance companies, are paying 26 per cent, 27 per cent or 28 per cent. Those who are forced to borrow through second mortgages, are in some cases paying up to 35 per cent.
It is an atrocious situation when we have to put up with a government with another three years to go which is dedicated to high interest rates and more deficits. This government has no fiscal policy to speak of and it cannot defend this policy.
If we consider some of the rates in other countries and make a comparison of the inflation rates, we can see some of the areas in which we have gone wrong. In Canada we have a prime rate of 19.5 per cent with an inflation rate of 13.9 per cent, and rising. That is the bad feature. Our interest rates are going up while the interest rates in other countries are going down.
The United States at present has a prime interest rate of 20.5 per cent with an inflation rate of 10.2 per cent, and many economists suggest it is going down. If it does, it will pull ours along with it, as is usually the case when that economy recovers.
Germany has a prime interest rate of 12 per cent-and many businesses there are unhappy about that rate-with an inflation rate of only 5.6 per cent. That is a country which 35 years ago was ravished, with nothing left of its business community.
Japan has a prime interest rate of around 7 per cent with an inflation rate of 6.2 per cent. That country was also ravished, perhaps even worse than Germany in some respects.
I find it very strange that about one year ago the governor of the Bank of Canada stood before the committee on finance and said, "I will not allow the inflation rate to go to 15 per cent; under no conditions will I allow it". The rate is now almost at 14 per cent and is going up. What has happened to the governor of the Bank of Canada? I suggest he is simply following the instructions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). The Minister of Finance has no alternative, because of the deficits of this government but to keep interest rates high in order to encourage investors to buy Government of Canada bonds.
Government borrowings now account for over 50 per cent of all borrowing in Canada compared to 25 per cent 15 years ago. In the last seven years we have had over $20 billion in deficits. In this current year we have a $14 billion deficit, but the government is telling us it is going down. 1 do not believe that. Government spending is going up by 16 per cent this year. We know the estimates the government provides are not true estimates. If you or I as an individual were to show an expense of $7,000 on our income tax return, the Department of Revenue would assume that was a true expense. If we had $3,000 in revenue which we applied against those expenses, they would not be true expenses. Our expenses then should be $10,000. That is what the government is doing with its estimates. It uses the netting effect. What we see as government expenditures of approximately $61 billion is not a true figure; it is false. Of the $3.8 billion we are paying out for imported oil, the government is showing approximately $500 million. It is not showing the true figures, and this sort of thing goes on and on in the estimates. This is the netting effect. This is not a $61 billion or $64 billion expenditure, it is something more like $80 billion or $90 billion.
Once again the government does not want the people of Canada to know this and it says it will look after it. The government is spending approximately 25 per cent more than it is taking in. This is unbelievable, but it has been doing it for years. About 20 cents of every dollar the government takes in is used just to service debt. The government has no intention of ever paying off its debts. How could a small business or an individual operate like that? The government would never allow them to do that.
Just last week I did an analysis of the money supply in Canada and its relationship to inflation. In the mid-1970s the government told us it would have to control the rate of growth of the money supply-which is credit-so that it could control inflation. But when we control the money supply, there is a tendency for interest rates to go up. The government kept telling us that this would benefit us because inflation would be controlled. I have figures here for the last ten years. In only one year, 1977, when the money supply decreased did inflation go down. In four years the money supply increased and inflation decreased. In three years the money supply decreased and inflation increased. In two years the money supply increased and inflation also increased. We cannot control inflation by controlling the money supply unless we can control government spending. That is why this monetary policy of the
May 25, 1981

government does not work, and that is why small businesses have problems. They do not have access to many lenders. There is only one lender to which they go.
I hate to think of the legacy this Prime Minister is leaving behind. I am afraid the Liberal party will never recover. When this Prime Minister leaves this chamber, members of the Liberal party will be telling us they have new policies and new leaders. It will be the same old story. There will be large deficits, high interest rates and many bankruptices. The small business community is being ignored. Its profits are decreasing. It is not able to finance properly. Seven times in the last five elections this Prime Minister has stood before the people of Canada and said "I will control government spending". Government spending has increased from $500 million in deficits in 1968 to $14 billion annually in 1981. I do not know anyone in Canada who should believe the Prime Minister and the Liberal party, least of all the small business community.
There have been 11 increases in the price of gasoline and heating oil over the past year. Those prices have increased over 50 per cent. Those increases have been presided over by a government which said it would keep gasoline prices down. This government bought heavy oil, unseen, from Mexico. It cannot be refined at Canadian refineries. This government does not know what it is doing.
There are 1.1 million small businesses in Canada. They account for over 66 per cent of the employment and job creation in Canada. The small business community provides more opportunities for both skilled and unskilled labour than any other industry.
In 1979 the Canadian Federation of Independent Business surveyed 9,000 small businesses. Five of the most serious problems cited were, first, finance; second, inflation; third, shortage of skilled help; fourth, government regulation and paper work; and fifth, taxation. I would like to review a couple of these.
The small business development bond was introduced by the Conservative government. Fortunately the Liberal government decided to continue that program. It is a very favourable type of borrowing for small businesses. The terms are good, up to five years. The rate is approximately one half of prime, and small businesses can borrow amounts ranging from $10,000 to $0.5 million. However, small businesses were asked recently why they do not borrow from the small business development bond, and they replied that small businesses have considered, but rejected, government-backed loans because of the danger of becoming entangled in bureaucratic red tape. That red tape keeps getting worse and worse.
Small businesses are particularly hard hit by inflation. There is no question that large businesses can cut back on their inventories in certain areas, but small businesses cannot. There is no question that one of the major problems small businesses are having right now is the high cost of financing their inventories. In few areas other than the area of small business
Small Business
can one say that high financing costs will defeat a business so easily. Small businesses must finance to carry inventories.
Another concern of small business people is government regulation and paper work. Businessmen have told me that 20 per cent of their time is taken up by government regulation and paper work. Even the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) admits that there is too much paper work. I was astounded to hear him say this afternoon that there is a six-year limit on the retention of documents. That will not help relieve the paper burden. Having been involved in storing documents in a business for many years, I can tell the House that once documents are put away, they are put away. The biggest problem is the amount of paper which must be gathered each year and put away. The documents which are put aside do not take up anything but space. That is a cost to a business, but it is a minor cost compared with the cost of the time spent doing paper work. This minister tells us he is helping small business, but he really has not solved the problem. He had a lot of gall to say what he said this afternoon.
1 am going to present three recommendations to the government tonight. The Minister of Finance is always saying in this House that the opposition never makes any suggestions. The problem is that he is not listening. If I had my way, I would cancel the national energy policy completely. There is no question that that damned policy is ruining Canadians. It accounts for the high interest rates we have right now. Let me explain briefly why. Approximately two billion exploration dollars are leaving the country, and money will continue to leave the country over the next five years. It is not hard to find many businesses in Canada which do nothing else but raise money for Canadian drilling companies drilling in the United States. They are still doing it. It is estimated that the figure is up to $2 billion. I have spoken with representatives of firms which do this, and they have told me that they will raise $2 billion in total each year for the next five years. Fifty per cent of all the drilling rigs which operated in Canada last year are now in the United States, and they are being supported by funds from Canada. That is one of the reasons we have high interest rates.
With respect to the export of natural gas, natural gas firms in western Canada have stated on more than one occasion- and have proved it-that they can export up to 50 per cent more natural gas than they are exporting right now, but the price of natural gas is tied to the price of imported oil. Every time the price of imported oil increases, so does the price of natural gas. Those prices should not be tied. Natural gas has nothing to do with imported oil. It is not an import. We are exporting natural gas. We have to get away from the formula which ties the price of natural gas to the price of imported crude oil. In 1980 we exported $4 billion worth of natural gas. And that, these firms are telling us, is 50 per cent of what they could do. This is a very serious problem because we are not talking about multinationals but about small Canadian firms which have locked themselves in gas wells for a minimum of five years and they do not know what they are going to do. I

May 25, 1981
Small Business
can tell you what they are going to do: they are going to persist until they can no longer finance the wells and then they will be taken over by the governments. That is what this government wants to do. It will buy up these shut-in gas wells for 25 per cent of their real value, which is the value put on them right now by the banks. They are prepared to give credit for 25 per cent of the real value because they will be shut in for up to five years.
My last suggestion to the Liberals is that the government bring in a program related to mortgage interest and property tax credits. I was not here when the Conservative government brought in this policy, but of all the things I have seen this seemed to make the most sense because it has the immediate effect of reducing the financing costs of the average home owner by at least 3 to 4 per cent. My calculations suggest at least that, but it could perhaps be higher depending on the tax bracket. However, surely this government can bend a little on policy and recognize a few of the excellent programs the Conservative government brought in. There are 500,000 home owners renewing their mortgages this year. They just cannot go on with this.
The Minister of Finance was, for lack of a better term, sucked in by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) on a program to nationalize the oil industry. There is no other word for it. You can talk to the staff in his department and they will tell you that they have a policy to nationalize the oil industry. If you want to read some of the books of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), it says right there that the way to socialize or nationalize this country is to make sure that private industry does not work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF FAILURE TO ASSIST SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add my voice to this debate. My constituency has a large number of small businesses, and we value them very highly. I am sure that everyone realizes the answers to our economic problems are not simple ones. They are complex problems and we do not want to be like that great knight Sir Ronald, the hero in Stephen Leacock's novel, who jumped upon his horse and rode off in all directions.
The question of who invented the small business development bond reminds me of the story about who invented the telephone. They finally came to the conclusion that the answer to this problem had to be that it was conceived in Brantford, Ontario and born in Boston. So I suppose that the small business development bond, we have to agree, was conceived
by the opposition when they were in power and was delivered by the Liberal government.
Now, I am somewhat disturbed when our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is criticized for his leadership in the North-South dialogue, and recently the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was criticized for his activities in the World Bank, and I would just like to draw to your attention the fact there is a very close relationship and dependency between the economy of the rich and poor countries of the world.
I would just like to read to you for the record from a supplement to the report of the Parliamentary Task Force on North-South Relations. North-South, what is it? Why should Canadians care? Here are some examples of the consequences which might befall us if the governments of north and south do not curtail and reverse the growth of world poverty. If there is a loan default by only one or two of the ten countries which account for 70 per cent of the $300 billion debt owed mainly to northern banks, the industrialized countries face the possibility of a full-fledged depression. Political instability, fed by massive poverty increases the likelihood one of those isolated skirmishes in the Third World will escalate into super power confrontation, causing us to spend more and more tax dollars fortifying our security systems. Let there be no doubt that there is a relationship.
I would now like to talk for a moment about the small business development bond. The opposition contends that this government has been insensitive to the plight of the small businessman who today faces a record high interest burden. However, these critics choose to belittle an extremely significant interest subsidy that was implemented by this government for small businesses. I am speaking of the small business development bond.
The measure was designed primarily to assist small businesses to expand their operations by enabling them to obtain loans at reduced interest rates to carry out such expansions. However, its scope is much broader than that. It is also designed to assist small businesses that are unable to meet their financial commitments by enabling them to reduce their interest burden.
This latter aspect of the program is often overlooked but can be an extremely important one. For example, let us assume that a small incorporated hardware store owes $100,000 to a bank in respect of the mortgage on the property in which the store carries on its business. The mortgage has come up for renewal and the applicable rate has increased from 10 per cent to 18 per cent. Unfortunately, the actual and expected profits of the business are inadequate to cover this increased expense. The result would be a mortgage foreclosure.
The hardware store in this instance can likely reduce its interest costs to the 10 per cent level on the old mortgage by using the SBDB measure. The paperwork involved is minimal. The store and its bank need only complete a single page election form in respect of the new mortgage and mail it to the Revenue Canada district taxation office to which the store normally mails its annual tax return.
May 25, 1981

As a result of making such an election, the bank will not be taxed on any interest it earns on the new mortgage. Thus it will earn after tax the same amount on the new mortgage by charging 9 per cent interest as it did on the old mortgage by charging 18 per cent. The administration costs associated with the procedure will probably result in the bank requesting a 10 or 11 per cent rate of return. This rate is not fixed by the government and is completely subject to negotiation by the borrower and the lender.
The bank in the above example does not lose anything by accepting the reduced interest rate since it is not taxed on it. On the contrary, it benefits by the fact the hardware store will be more likely to repay its loan. There is no government department or agency from which the bank or hardware store is required to obtain approval before such a loan is made. However, in practice, cautious lenders often take steps to obtain an assurance from Revenue Canada officials that the prerequisites for making a small business development bond loan are satisfied.
This device can be used by incorporated farmers whose carrying costs have reached unmanageable levels. Although care should be taken to consult the actual small business development bond rules in specific cases, one can say in general that any small incorporated Canadian active business with retained earnings which do not surpass $750,000 which is unable to repay a loan can utilize the small business development bond vehicle to slash its interest costs by almost 50 per cent on up to $500,000 of qualifying debt.
Undoubtedly the opposition will point out that the measure is not available for healthy corporations which, though hard hit by high interest rates, are able to handle their debt load. We acknowledge this fact, but we do not feel the need to apologize for it. The government's interest rate policy would be severely undermined if all small businesses were insulated from its effects. The assistance provided was reserved for those who needed it most.
However, in order to help our economy to recover its former strength and vigour, provision was made in the small business development bond program to assist all small businesses to expand their operations. Thus, even healthy businesses can benefit from the interest rate relief afforded by the program if they use the funds obtained to build new structures, to purchase new equipment, or to carry out scientific research and development. In this manner we hope to foster growth in our economy and to lower levels of unemployment. The measure was restricted to new capital asset purchases in an effort to stimulate simultaneously the manufacturing sector.
The opposition suggested that the measure be made available to unincorporated businesses. The nature of unincorporated businesses is such that it would be very difficult to ensure that borrowed funds were used for permitted purposes, since even the separation of business and personal assets is often unclear in the case of unincorporated businesses.
Small Business
Further, complex rules would be required to assess the smallness of an unincorporated business, whereas well-known rules already exist to accomplish this objective in respect of incorporated businesses.
I must also point out that the incorporation of the business is now a simple and relatively inexpensive operation. In addition, rules were provided in the small business development bond legislation to permit qualifying assets acquired by unincorporated businesses to qualify when transferred to a newly incorporated company. Further, the existing tax law permits assets to be transferred without tax costs into a new company. In the case of unincorporated farmers and small family businesses, it provides parallel treatment for the intergenerational transfer of shares of a family farm or small business corporation. Thus, there appears to be no valid reason to introduce further complexity into the small business development bond legislation by creating rules for unincorporated businesses.
The suggestion has also been made that the measure be expanded to cover working capital loans. The revenue costs associated with an unlimited expansion to working capital loans are very significant. Our estimates indicate that such costs could attain several million dollars. As indicated, the measure was not intended to be a general interest rate subsidy. Such a subsidy would conflict with the government's over-all policy to reduce inflation. It was designed solely to provide relief in those cases where it was most needed, that is where there was genuine financial difficulty, and most desirable, that is where capital expansion and scientific research were to be done. The preceding considerations are equally applicable to all businesses. There is no justification for an extension of the measure to cover the inventory carrying costs of one particular business group.
Although we are unable to provide actual figures, all our sources in the financial community indicate that the small business development bond program has been very widely used by small businesses in all regions of the country and that it can only, at this point in time, be categorized as an unqualified success.
To summarize, it is erroneous to say that the government has failed to assist the small business sector in Canada. It is true that no general interest rate subsidy was made available to the small business sector. However, as indicated previously, relief was provided in those cases where it was most needed and most desirable. A general interest rate subsidy for the small business sector was not provided for two very important reasons. First, such a move would largely undermine the very purpose which present interest rates are intended to serve. Second, such a program would likely cost the government and taxpayers several hundred million dollars. We are not prepared to adopt such a course of action at this time.
In so far as the possible extension of the program is concerned, such a decision requires that we carefully assess whether there is a continued need for the program and whether it is cost effective. It is much too early to attempt to predict whether there will be a need for the program next year. Further, the data required to assess the cost effectiveness of

That is why interest rates are between 23 and 25 per cent at the Federal Business Development Bank. That is why we have two situations occurring throughout the country. We have big business able to swallow up the little guys because it has the credit to go to the banks and borrow the money for takeovers, while small business can either try to pass the cost of credit on to consumers or go bust. And the very nature of small business is that there are a number of little fellows in the game competing with one another. The result of this high interest rate policy is that only the very strong will survive-the weak will perish and prices will rise.
When the government says that this interest rate policy is an anti-inflation policy, it is really saying that it is a big business policy, a high price policy-a policy in favour of inflation.
