speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to a question I put to him on April 13 about missing documents in the Taschereau-Mackenzie King papers, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) indicated to me, as reported at page 9197 of Hansard, without so much as batting an eyelid, that his interest in the question was more historical than political because, he said, the loss of one of Mackenzie King's diaries was recorded years ago.
Has it occurred to him to be a little curious about why the diary should have disappeared in 1947? Is he so sure that the Taschereau documentation is complete? If that documentation reveals gaps, what does he propose to do?
Is the man naive? Has he learned nothing from interwar history, or more particularly, from post-war history? Does he give no credence to what those outstanding Russian dissidents, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn and Andrei Sakharov have been saying about Soviet threats to the west for the past decade or so-not the nuclear threat, but the threat to our social fabric and to our economic organization that the Soviet Union and its workers are set on destroying one way or another? Does he discount such pleas, such urgings, such warnings as mere rhetoric spawned in the minds of overwrought neurotics? Has he written Solzhenitsyn and Sakharov off as kooks? He is ready enough to charge the Soviet Union with bad faith when it comes to mistreating their citizens and denying exit permits to the Shumok's and the Shcharansky's of this world. Why does he refuse to believe the Soviet Union when it says to the West, "We'll bury you"? Why should he berate them in one instance and be ready to exonerate them in the other?
Has he read Sakharov's "Letter from Exile" written in exile in Gorky in May, 1980, and smuggled out of the Soviet Union to appear in print in the New York Times Magazine Supplement on June 8, 1980? Does he consider that Sakharov is a raving lunatic when he lists the four groups of citizens in the west who, by reason of their positions in government, in the industrial sector and in the media, are able to promote Soviet influence and expansionist goals? Or does he hold that the Sakharov letter is a forgery? He may have forgotten that Gouzenko said as much in a letter published on October 12, 1968, in the Congressional Record, 20 years after giving evidence in Ottawa.
Why should he think Canada is immune from subversion? Does the loss of documents relating to subversion not make him feel just a little, tiny bit uncomfortable? Is he really

May 25, 1981
Adjournment Debate
concerned with history and with personal privacy, as he says in answer to my supplementary question? Has he not thought of the implications of the losses for the nation's security? How has he come to convince himself, given the loss of strategic documentation, and for other reasons, that there are no moles at work at various levels in Canada's government service? Strategically important documents do not disappear on their own. They need a helping hand. Whose hand was at work and is it still at work? Is he not concerned about the apparent indifference of the government in determining whether those moles are not still burrowing away? Where are they located or is he so blind because he has been hoodwinked into believing there are no such moles? How naive can the Solicitor General be? Has it not struck him and the Canadian people that, since 1945, Canada is the only major western country which has not had a first-rate spy scandal? To what do we owe this special immunity? I lay this at the door of the government's indifference. It is purblindness or even perversity, whichever is the worst. There may even be a more sinister explanation. Are those moles in Canada being protected by persons in positions of influence?
Britain has had its Philbys, its Burgesses and its MacLeans. More recently it has had its Blunts, and now a shadow is cast over another prominent British secret agent. The Germans have had their problems too, as have the U.S.A. and Australia. Are Canadians such dedicated patriots that we have prevented infiltration entirely? That is difficult to credit. Given our strategic position geographically and politically in the western world, Canada cannot be anything else but a prime target for infiltration and subversion unless, of course, suspicion about our moles had made our friends unwilling to show us any vital secrets. I fear for the future of this country when I am obliged to note the attitude of this government to the live threat confronting us. I am at a loss to know how to shake it up. I am the more fearful when I recall that 35 years ago, the Tas-chereau report of the Gouzenko investigation mentioned the presence of several spy rings in Canada and referred to the difficulty in identifying the members of more than one of them, namely the Zabotin Ring-

Mr. Speaker, we could be here all night if we all attempted to address the broad issues raised by the hon. gentleman opposite. Therefore, I shall restrict my remarks specifically to one portion of his address, namely the Taschereau commission papers.
I am pleased to respond to the question raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). In his question of April 13, 1981, the hon. member asked several questions relating to the so-called missing Taschereau commission
papers and the so-called missing Mackenzie King diaries. Specifically, the hon. member asked why the minister and his colleagues were "so indifferent to the disappearance of these documents." He also asked for an assurance that an inquiry was taking place within the department and in the department of the Secretary of State, "to make sure every possible clue is being followed up to find out where these documents might be." The minister has asked officials in his department and in other departments of the Government of Canada to attempt to determine the exact composition and present disposition of the documentation relating to the Taschereau commission and the papers of the late prime minister.
It has been determined that there are four known copies of the transcripts of the Taschereau-Kellock royal commission. One copy is divided into ten volumes with two indices and comprises the testimony of 110 witnesses recorded in 6,042 pages. This copy was retained by the Privy Council office until 1963, and then transferred to the Public Archives. It was retrieved by the Privy Council office in 1976 for examination, and returned again in 1978 to the Public Archives. It was withdrawn once again by the Privy Council office in March, 1981, and is the document currently under review for the purposes of eventual publication. This document is complete, and there are no missing sections.
Copies two and three are divided into 49 volumes and both are located at the RCMP archives. These documents are complete. I wish to notify hon. members that the exhibits and miscellaneous papers of the Taschereau-Kellock commission, involving some 601 original statements, personal notebooks of persons interviewed by the commission, etc., are also stored in RCMP archives.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, I asked a question of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) about the award of a fire engine contract in connection with the Walter Truck affair. The contract has been awarded to the Walter Truck Canada Company, and I thought that I had found certain facts which deserved the attention of the House. The Department of National Defence needed these special crash trucks and the order amounted to $6 million for 32 trucks. The lowest bidder was the firm les Camions Pierre Thibault Inc., of Pierreville, in Quebec, which has a well-established reputation, good Canadian content and the required expertise.
The second lowest bidder was the Walter Truck Canada Company, from Ville D'Ajou, in Quebec. This company was
May 25, 1981

purchased at the time when the bids were submitted, it had never built fire engines such as those requested and it had neither the staff nor the expertise required when the bid was made. The only thing they had in hand were the plans for a fire truck almost identical to that requested, and indeed the plans were bought from a bankrupt American company. If I may be allowed a comparison, let us say that the Walter Truck Company, at the time of tendering, was as well equipped as any private individual in Canada having in hand the plans for a warship which would meet the requirements of a Supply and Services order. That individual could be awarded the contract without any previous experience in shipbuilding. The least we could say is that such tendering practices are unbelievable. To my supplementary question in this House, the minister answered as follows, and I quote:
-the contract was awarded to the Walter Truck Canada Company because it did guarantee more Canadian content than the lowest bid which was rejected.
In a press interview, the president of the Walter Truck Company, Mr. Georges Laporte, stated on November 11, 1980, he had the plans from an American company and the Canadian content was only 62 per cent, while the Thibault trucks had a 70 per cent content.
As the saying goes in trade talk, it is the pump that makes the fire truck. The Walter pump is made in the U.S.A., while the Thibault pump is manufactured here in Canada. The Pierre Thibault company have been manufacturing all kinds of fire trucks for more than 72 years. The Walter Truck Canada Company is a recently established firm which as of the time tenders were called had never built anything else but snow-plows.
The thought of questioning the integrity of our officials never occurred to me. I was myself a civil servant for ten years and I am sure that they correctly performed the work that they were asked to do. However, one may wonder whether at the time tenders were called there was not a lack of information or at least of flexibility which did not allow for a more serious perusal of that tender nor a greater stress on the benefit of experience, technique and the more competitive prices of Pierre Thibault Inc.
Last Thursday, in reply to a question I asked him, the Minister of Supply and Services said that Walter Truck Canada had a greater Canadian content than Pierre Thibault Inc., that being one of the reasons why it was chosen.
Now, I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have left, that that argument simply does not hold water. This company's Canadian content is only 62 per cent. Thibault, on the other hand, states that the Canadian content of its trucks is 70 per cent. Is it the kind of Canadian content that is considered?
This is the answer the minister gave to my first question, and I quote:
-the bids filed were very thoroughly examined.
I wonder, in closing, Mr. Speaker, whether the minister would consider asking for a review by an independent

HUMAN RIGHTS AND INDIAN AFFAIRS-1. INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN WOMEN. 2. REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN BAND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 6 I asked the Secretary of State for External

May 25, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) about Canada's commitment to the United Nation's Human Rights Committee. Last November Canada indicated to the committee that it would introduce legislation by mid-1981 to end the discrimination against Indian women which now exists under the Indian Act.
In response to my question, the minister referred once again to his "powers under the Indian Act to set aside those provisions which discriminate against status women who marry white men and lose their status" whenever a band chief and council passed resolutions asking him to do so. The minister said:
We have received some of these resolutions now, and I am acting on them.
That same day, April 6, 1981, in response to a question asked in the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development on April 2, 1981, a departmental official wrote:
Unfortunately we have not been able to act on any of these requests. Simply removing application of Section 12(l)(b) will not achieve the minister's objective of placing Indian women who marry non-Indians on equal footing with Indian men who marry non-Indians. The Department of Justice has not as yet been able to determine which sections can be removed to achieve this goal.
Obviously when the minister promised to use Section 4 of the Indian Act to get around the ugly fact of discrimination, he was either perpetrating a fraud or he did not know what he was talking about.
In the same way, the Department of External Affairs deceived the United Nations Human Rights Committee when it suggested mid-1981 as the time when legislation would be introduced to eliminate this discrimination. On May 12 when the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development appeared before the committee, he finally admitted that there would be no such legislation by mid-1981. Rather, he talked about a three-year period while we are waiting for the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to come into effect.
I would be interested in knowing if Canada is going to revise the answer it gave to the United Nations Human Rights Committee. In November the government said to that committee that the legislation would be tabled by mid-1981. Last summer the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that Indian women would have to wait one or two years more for justice. Now the minister tells us not to worry and that we have a period of three years to find a solution to this problem. Is Canada going to go to the United Nations and inform it about this change in its intentions? I agree with the minister that the problem is complex and that in our desire to do justice to Indian women we do not want to ride roughshod over the rights of the Indian people as a whole. But the Canadian government's failure to act will not make the problem go away. Instead, it will continue to fester until it erupts in a manner which will hurt all Indian people.
We in our party do not want to see a solution imposed. We hope that by a process of negotiation, this discrimination can
be eliminated quickly without doing violence to the Indian people. More and more of the Indian people themselves, both men and women, are speaking up on this matter and urging that the government take action.
My question is: when will the government show some leadership and some initiative to end this discrimination? Or is it going to continue a policy of drift and indecision and of promising one thing to the United Nations, something else to the House of Commons and something else again to the Indian people? I fear that unless the government does show leadership, it will end up with a crisis on its hands and it will act in a stupid, unthinking manner which will only make matters worse.
When will the government show some leadership and sit down with Indian organizations, including Indian women's organizations, to erase this black mark against human rights in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, Canada's response to the questions from the United Nations Human Rights Committee arising from the submission of Sandra Lovelace and her loss of Indian status as a result of her marriage to a non-Indian under section 12(1 )(b) of the Indian Act was forwarded by the Government of Canada in November, 1980. In the course of that response, the federal government outlined the nature of the situation facing Indian women marrying non-Indian men and, in particular, referred to statements made by Ms Lovelace herself concerning her relationships with the Tobique Indian Band Council, particularly in respect of housing on the reserve.
In addition, the question of what steps the Government of Canada was contemplating in respect of section 12(1 )(b) was asked. The government's reply indicated that there was a commitment to end discrimination based upon sex against Indian women, and further outlined that any future revisions to the Indian Act would address this question in such a way that provisions in the act would apply equally to both Indian men and Indian women.
Some of the proposed items under consideration were referred to as well as the fact that additional revision concerning local Indian band government was also being considered at this time. The nature of this legislation which my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), has referred to on a number of occasions in this chamber would be enabling legislation under which individual Indian bands could choose to operate under a newly legislated form of Indian government giving them responsibility and authority for their own social, economic and cultural development at the local band level.
The response to the United Nations Human Rights Committee specifically stated that one of the items being considered under that enabling legislation referred to band control over membership. It is anticipated that any such band control would also be exercised on the basis of the application of uniform, non-discriminatory bylaws concerning membership.
